ENARRATIONS ON THE PSALMS III
HISTORY, CONSOLATION OF THE PERSECUTED PEOPLE] SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1 [v.lj. In the frontispiece of this psalm it is written: For the end, in favor of Iditho; psalm for Asaph. What is for the end? You already know it. The end of the law is Christ, in order to justice, for every believer. Iditho means the one who passes through them, and Asaf, congregation or gathering. Then the congregation speaks here that goes through to reach the end, which is Christ Jesus. What are the things that must be traversed so that we can reach that end where we will no longer have anywhere else to traverse? The very text of the psalm declares it. We must indeed continue to go through everything that prevents us, everything that embarrasses us, everything that chains us with some bond until we reach what is enough for us, and where beyond which there is nothing, and below it are all things and therefore they are all things. Philip wanted to see the Father, and he said to our Lord Jesus Christ: Show us the Father, and that is enough for us, as if for a long time he would have to go through something other than Him until he reached the Father, in which he would be safely situated and would not have to look for anything further from Him; for this is what he implied when he said: and it is enough for us. However, He who had said in all truth: I and the Father are one, admonished Philip and taught every man to understand who Christ is and that the end was also in Him, because He and the Father are one.

1 {v.l]. Psalmi huius limen ita inscribitur: In finem, pro Idithun, Psalmus ipsi Asaph. In finem quid sit, nostis: Finís enim Legis Christus ad iustitiam omni credenti (Rom 10,4). Idithun interpretatur Transiliens eos; Asaph interpretatur Congregatio. Loquitur hic ergo congregationtio transiliens, ut perveniat ad finem qui est Christus lesus. Quae sint itaque transilienda, ut ad illum finem pervenire possimus, ubi iam quod transiliamus non habebimus, Psalmi textus ipse demonstrat. Etenim tamdiu transilire debenmus quidquid nos impedit, quidquid irretit, quidquid visco quodam illigat, et onere aggravat volatum nostrum, doñee perveniamus ad id quod sufficit, ultra quod nihil est, infra quod sunt omnia, et ex quo sunt omnia. Patrem quippe ipsum volebat Philippus intueri, et dicebat Domino Iesu Christo, Ostende nobis Patrem, et sufficit nobis; tanquam tamdiu illi transiliendum esset quidquid aliud esset, doñee perveniret ad Patrem, ubi iam securus assisteret, et quid ei ultra requirendum esset non haberet: hoc est enim, Sufficit. Verum ille qui verissime dixerat, Ego et Pater unum sumus (lo 10,30), admonuit Philippum, docuitque omnem hominem qui Christum intelligeret, etiam in eo habere finem,

same thing. That is why he says to him: I have been with you for so long and you have not known me? Philip, he who sees me, sees the Father. Therefore, whoever wants to perceive, imitate and retain the spirit of this psalm, let him pass through all carnal things, trample underfoot the attractions and honor of this world and look for nothing else to rest on except him for whom all things are and in whom he also works until he reaches the end. What does this one that passes through reveal to us? 2 [v. 2]. With my voice, he says, I cried out to the Lord. Many cry out to the Lord in order to achieve wealth and avoid harm. They cry out for the health of their loved ones, for the stability of their home, for temporal happiness, for worldly dignity, in short, for physical health itself, which is the heritage of the poor. For this and other similar things many cry out to the Lord, but hardly any cry out for the Lord Himself. It is very common for man to desire anything from the Lord and not desire Him himself, as if what He gives could be more pleasant than Him who gives it. Anyone who cries out to the Lord for anything outside of Him is not yet a soul. What does this one say that goes through? With my voice I cried to the Lord. So that you do not think that whoever uttered the voice uttered it for anything other than the Lord, he then adds: and my voice was addressed to God. The voice with which we cry out to God is uttered, but this voice is directed to something else, not to God. This is what the voice is directed towards by what it has been uttered. But this one who freely loved God, who offered a voluntary sacrifice to the quia ipse et Pater unum sunt: ​​Tanto, inquit, tempore vobiscum sum, et non vidistis me? Philippe, qui me videt, videt et Vatrem (ibid. 14,8.9). Quisquís ergo psalmi huius animum sentimentale, imitari, tenere vult, omnia desideria carnalia transiliat, saeculique huius pompam et illecebram calcet, nihilque sibi aliud proponat ubi consistat, nisi ex quo sunt omnia: in quibus ómnibus etiam ipse laborat doñee ad finem perveniat. Quid nobis ergo indicat iste transiliens? 2 [v.2]. Voce mea, inquit, ad Dominum clamavi. Sed multi clamant ad Dominum pro divitiis acquirendis damnisque devitandis, pro suorum salute, pro stabilitate domus suae, pro felicítate temporali, pro dignitate saeculari; desserto pro ipsa etiam salute corporis, quae patrimonium est pauperis.

Pro his atque buiusmodi rebus multi clamant ad Dominum; vix quisquam propter ipsum Dominum. Facile quippe homini est quodlibet desiderare a Domino, et ipsum Dominum non desiderare; quasi vero suavius ​​esse possit quod dat, quam ipse qui dat. Quisquís ergo pro alia re qualibet clamat ad Dominum, nondum est transiliens. Hic vero transiliens quid dícit? Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi. Et ne arbitreris vocem ipsius qua clamavit ad Dominum, propter aliud emissam quam propter ipsum Dominum, secutus ait: Et vox mea ad Deum. Emittitur enim vox qua clamemus ad Deum, et ipsa vox ad aliud est, non ad Deum. Ad hoc enim est vox, propter quod editur vox. Iste vero qui Deum gratis amarat, qui voluntarie Deo sacribat (Ps 53,8), qui transilierat quidquid infra est, nihilque aliud
History, consolation for the persecuted people

Lord, who had destroyed everything that was under God and who saw nothing above him where he could empty his soul except in him, from him and for him by whom he had been created, to whom he cried out with his voice, since he had uttered it for him, says: my voice is addressed to God. And maybe for no reason? Hear what's next: and he attended to me. Without a doubt he helps you when you look for him, but not when you look for something else for him. It was said of certain individuals that they called and there was no one to save them; (they cried) to the Lord and he did not hear them. Because? Because his voice was not directed to the Lord. This is stated elsewhere in Scripture where, speaking of such, it says: they did not call on the Lord. They did not stop crying; However, they did not call on the Lord. What does it mean they did not call on the Lord? They did not call on the Lord to be theirs, that is, they did not invite the Lord to enter their heart; They did not want the Lord to dwell in them. And so what happened to them? There they trembled with fear where there was no fear. They trembled at the loss of the things present, because they were not filled with him whom they called upon. They did not love him for free so that they could say in the face of the loss of temporal things: as it pleased God, so it was done; Blessed be the name of the Lord. Then this one says here: my voice addressed the Lord, and he attended to me. Let him show us how it happens. 3 [v. 3]. In the day of my tribulation I sought God. You, who are you, that you do this? See what you earnestly seek in the day of your tribulation. If prison troubles you, you look for a way to get out of it; If the fever bothers you, you seek health; si el supra se viderat quo effunderet animam suam, nisi ex quo, et per quem, et in quo creatus erat, ad quem clamaverat voce sua, ad illum esse fecerat ipsam vocem suam: Vox mea, inquit, ad Deum. Et numquid sine causa? Vide quid sequitur: Et attendit mihi. Veré tune tibi attendit, quando ipsum quaeris, non quando per ipsum aliud quaeris. Dictum est de quibusdam: Clamaverunt, neo erat qui salvos faceret, ad Dominum, nec exaudivit eos (Ps 17,42). Quare? Quia vox eorum non ad Dominum. Exprimit hoc alio loco Scriptuia, ubi dicit de talibus: Dominum non invokeverunt. Ad illum clamare non cessaverunt; et tamen Dominum non invokeverunt. Quid est, Dominum non invokeverunt? Dominum in se non vocaverunt: ad cor suum Dominum non invitationverunt; Domino is inhabited noluerunt. Et idea quid eis contigit?

Ibi trepidaverunt timore, ubi non erat timor (Ps 13:5). Ideo de rerum praesentium amissione tremuerunt, quoniam non erant pleni illo quem non invocation. Non gratis amaverunt, ut amissis temporalibus rebus possent dicere: Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est; sit nomen Domini benedictum (Iob 1,21). Ergo iste, Vox mea, inquit, ad Dominum, et attendit mihi. Doceat nos quomodo id fiat. 3 [v.3]. In die tribulationis meae Deum exquisivi. Quis es, qui hoc facis? In die tribulationis tuae, vide quid exquiras. Si carcer facit tribulationem, exire de carcere exquiris: si febris facit tribulationem, sanitatem exquiris: si fames facit tribulationem,, saturitatem exquiris: si damna fa-

Hunger causes you discomfort, you see how to satisfy yourself; If temporary damage tortures you, you seek profit; If pilgrimage torments you, you rest in the city of your flesh. Why should I remember all things, or rather, how should I commemorate them all? Do you want to be the man through? In the day of your tribulation seek God; But do not seek anything else for God, but from tribulation set out to seek God, so that God may take tribulation away from you so that you may surely be united to him. In the day of my tribulation I sought God. Not anything else apart from him, but God. And how did you look for him? With my hands (directed) towards him at night. Say it again; Let's see, let's understand, let's imitate if we can. What did you seek in the day of your tribulation? Bye bye. How did you look for him? With my hands, you say. When did you look for him? At night. How did you look for him? Heading towards him. With what result did you search for him? I was not disappointed. Brethren, let us study all these things, let us consider them all, examine them; and let us also examine what the tribulation is, in which he sought God, and what it means to seek God with the hands, at night and towards him. Now he goes on to say what everyone understands: and I was not disappointed. What does it mean and I wasn't disappointed? I found what I was looking for. 4. No tribulation should be thought of. Indeed, he who does not go through, thinks that there is no more tribulation than that which occurs only due to some sad temporary event, but he who goes through judges tribulation all his life. For he loves the eternal homeland in such a way that the very earthly pilgrimage serves as a great tribulation for him. Please tell me of what ciunt tribulationem, lucrum exquiris: si peregrinado facit tribulationem, civitatem tuae carnis exquiris. Et quid cuneta commemorem, aut quando cuneta commemorem? Vis esse transiliens? In die tribulationis tuae Deum exquire: non per Deum aliud, sed ex tribulatione Deum; ut ad hoc Deus removeat tribulationem, ut securus inhaereas Deo. In die tribulationis meae Deum exquisivi: non aliud aliquid, sed Deum exquisivi? Et quomodo exquisisti? Manibus meis night coram eo. Die hoc rursus: videoamus, intelligamus, imitatemur, si possumus. In die tribulationis tuae quid exquisitesti? Deum. How exquisite? Manibus meis. When exquisite; Night. Ubi exquisite? Corameo. Et quo fructu exquisisti? Et non sum deceptus.

Omnia ergo videamus, fratres, omnia considermus, omnia interrogemus; et quid sit tribulatio, in qua iste Deum exquisivit, et quid sit manibus inquirere Deum, et quid sit nocte, et quid sit coram illo: et sequitur, quod omnes intelligunt, Et non sum deceptus. Quid est enim, Et non sum deceptus? Inveni quod quaerebam. 4. Tribulatio non illa vel illa cogitanda est. Etenim unusquisque nondum transiliens, nondum putat esse tribulationem, nisi quae acciderit huic vitae ex aliquo trísti tempore: at vero ille transiliens, totam vitam istam tribulationem suam reputat. Sic enim amat patriam supernam, ut terrena pilgrimage ipsa sit maxima tribulatio. Quomodo enim non sit

Isn't this life a tribulation? How can what is called continual temptation not be tribulation? In the book of Job it is recorded: Is not human life on earth a temptation? Did he say that human life on earth is tempted? No, because he said that life itself is temptation. Therefore, if it is temptation, it is tribulation. In this tribulation, that is, in this life this one who goes through sought God. As? With my hands, he says. What are your hands? His works. I was not looking for something corporeal so that I could find by feeling what I had lost; so that he could find the money, the gold, the silver, the clothing, everything that is of such a condition that it can be taken with the hands. Although our Lord Jesus Christ certainly wanted to be sought with the hands when, doubting, the disciple showed the scars, did it happen when he, touching the scars of the wounds, exclaimed: My Lord and my God, he did not hear: because you saw, you believed; Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed? Then if he, seeking Christ with his hands, deserved to hear this, so that having thus sought Christ was a dishonor to him, we who were called blessed because we believed without seeing, what shall we say? Will it not be our turn to search for Christ with our hands? It belongs to us to search; but, as I said, with the works. And when? At night. What does it mean at night? In this world. For it is night until the day shines with the glorious coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Do you want to see what it's like at night? If here in this world we did not have a lamp, we would remain in darkness, for Saint Peter says: We have the prophetic word as more certain, to which tribulatio vita ista, rogo vos? quomodo non sit tribulatio, quae dicta est tota tentatio? Habes scriptum in libro Iob: Numquid non tentatio est vita humano super terram? (ib. 6,1). Numquid dixit: Tentatur vita humano super terram? Ipsa vita tentatio est: si ergo tentatio, utique tribulatio. In hac igitur tribulatione, hoc est in hac vita, Deum exquisivit iste transiliens. What's up? Manibus, inquit, meis. Quid est, manibus meis? Operibus meis. Non enim aliquid corporeum quaerebat, ut contrectando inveniret quod perdiderat; ut manibus quaereret nummum, aurum, argentum, vestem, quidquid tale est quod manibus teneri possit. Quanquam et ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus voluit se manibus inquirí, quando dubitanti disciple scars otendit.

Sed numquid cum ille exclamasset tangens scars vulnerum eius, Dominus meus et Deus meus! nonne audivit: Quia vidisti, credidisti; beati qui non viderunt et crediderunt? (20,27-29). Si ergo ille manibus quaerens Christum, hoc audire meruit, ut opprobrium ei fuerit ita quaesisse; nos qui beati dicti sumus qui non vidimus et credimus, quid ergo, ad nos non pertinet manibus quaerere? Pertinet, sicut dixi, operibus quaerere. When hoc? Night. What is it, night? In hoc saeculo. Nox enim est antequam effulgeat dies in adventuclarato Domini nostri lesu Christi. Nam vultis videre quia nox est? Nisi luzernam hic haberemus, in tenebris permaneremus. Petrus enim dicit: Et nos habemus certiorem propheticum sermonem, cui bene facitis intendentes, velut Lucernae Lucenti in obscuro loco, doñee dies

You do well to pay attention, like a lamp that shines in a dark place until the day breaks and the morning star appears in your hearts. Then laugh about coming the day after tonight. Meanwhile, don't miss the lamp tonight. And this is perhaps what we do now, since, in exposing these words of Scripture, we present the lamp to illuminate us this night; which must always be lit in your dwellings. For it is said to such: Do not quench your spirit. And as if explaining who he is referring to, he continues: do not despise the prophecy, that is, let the lamp always shine in you. However, this light is undoubtedly night compared to a certain ineffable day. The very life of the faithful compared to the life of the unbelievers is day. But how it is night itself, we have already said and demonstrated with the testimony of the apostle Saint Peter, who, likewise, also calls it a lamp and admonishes us about it, that we turn to it, that is, to the prophetic word until the day breaks and the morning star shines in your hearts. How day the life of the faithful is also in comparison with the life of the wicked is demonstrated by Saint Paul saying: Let us cast away from ourselves the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. As during the day, let's walk decently. Therefore we who now live honestly are in the day compared to those who live the life of the wicked. But the day of this life of believers is not enough for this Iditho; He also wants to go through this day until he reaches that day, where he has absolutely no fear of nocturnal temptation. For although the life of believers is day here, it is nevertheless a luzcat, et lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris (2 Pet 1:19). Venturus est ergo dies post istam noctem; interim in hac night luzern non desit. Et hoc est fortasse quod nunc facimus: has Litteras exposing, luzernam inferimus, ut ¡n hac nocte gaudeamus. Quae quidem debent accensa esse semper in domibus vestris. Talibus enim dicitur: Spiritum nolite exstinguere (1 Thess v.19). Et tanquam exponens quid diceret, secutus ait, Prophetiam nolite spernere: id est, luzern in vobis semper luzat. Et haec quidem lux in comparatione cuiusdam ineffabilis dici nox dicitur. Nam ipsa vita fideüum in comparatione vitae infidelium dies est.

Quomodo autem sit nox, iam diximus, et ostendimus Petri apostoli testimony: qui quidem etiam et luzernam nominavit, et de ipsa luzern nos admonuit ut intendamus ei, id est prophetico sermoni, doñee dies luzcat, et lucifer oriatur in cordibus nostris. Quomodo autem iam vita fideüum dies sit in comparatione vitae impiorum, Paulus ostendit: Abiiciamus, inquit, opera tenebrarum, et induamur arma lucis; sicut in die honeste ambulemus (Rom 13:12). Ergo honeste viventes, in comparatione vitae impiorum, in die sumus. Sed iste dies vitae fideüum non sufficit hule Idithun; transilire vult et istum diem, doñee veniat ad illum diem, ubi noctis tentationem nullam omnino formidet. Hic enim quamvis dies sit vita fideüum, tentatio est vita humano super terram (Iob 7,1). Nox, et dies: dies in comparisone infidelium; nox in comparisone Angelorum.

temptation human life on earth. It is night and it is day: day comparing it with the life of the infidels; night compared to the life of angels. Well, the angels have a day that we don't have yet. We already have what the infidels do not have, but we still lack what the angels have; We will have it when we are equal to them, which is promised to us in the resurrection. Then in this already day and still night: night in comparison of the coming day that we wait for; and day in comparison to the past night that we have renounced; On this day, I repeat, let us search for God in the night with our hands. Do not stop the works; let us seek God; let our desire not be vain. If we are on the road, let's take provisions so we can get there. Let us seek God with our hands; Well, even when we search in the night for whom we seek with our hands, yet we are not deceived because we search for him before him. What does it mean before him? Do not do your righteousness before men to be seen by them, otherwise you will have no reward from your Father. When you give alms, and these are the hands that seek God, do not blow, he says, the trumpet before you as the hypocrites do, but do alms in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will give you the reward. Then (I sought God) with my hands in the night before him, and I was not deceived. 5. Let us hear with the greatest care how many things this Iditho endured on this earth and on this night, and how he had in a certain sense the need to cross by stinging him and pulling his passions down so that it would be impossible for him to cross. My soul refused to be consoled. I was possessed of so much sadness here, that my soul Habent enim diem Angelí quem nos nondum habemus: iam nos habemus quem non habent infideles; sed nondum habent fideles quem Angelí habent: tune autem habebunt, cum erunt aequales Angelis Dei; quod illis in resurrection promissum est (Mt 22:30). In hac ergo iam die, et adhuc nocte; nocte in comparatione futuri diei quem desideramus, die in comparatione praeteritae noctis cui renuntiavimus: in hac ergo, inquam, nocte Deum requiramus manibus nostris. Non cessation opera; quaeramus Deum, non sit inane desiderium. Yes in via sumus, sumptus erogemus, ut pervenire possimus: manibus quaeramus Deum. Etsi nocte quaerimus quem manibus quaerimus, non decipimur quia "coram ipso" quaerimus.

What is "coram ipso"? Nolite faceré iustitiam vestram coram hominibus, ut videamini ab eis; alioqui non habebitis mercedem apud Patrem vestrum. "Cum ergo facis eleemosynam", ait, manus illae sunt quaerentes Deum, "noli tubicinare ante te, sicut hypocritae faciunt; sed sit eleemosyna tua in oceulto, et Pater tuus qui videt in oceulto, reddet tibí" (Mt 6,1.2.4). Ergo, "Manibus meis nocte coram eo et non sum deceptus." 5. Quanta tamen iste Idithun pertulerit in hac terra, et in hac nocte, et quomodo habuerit quodammodo transiliendi necessitatem, impingentibus atque pungentibus deorsum tribulationibus, ut necesse fuerit transilire, intentissime audiamus. Nega-vit consoleri anima mea. Tantum taedium

He closed himself off from all comfort. Where did this guy's sadness come from? Perhaps because his vineyard was stoned, or because the olive tree did not produce oil, or because the harvest was prevented by the rain? Where did this sadness come from? Hear it in another psalm; It is also his voice that speaks there: Sorrow took hold of me because of the sinners who abandoned your law. He says that he was affected with such great sadness by this type of evil that his soul refused to be consoled. Ennui had almost completely overwhelmed him, and sadness had completely submerged him irreparably; and for the same reason he refuses to be consoled. What was left for him, then? 6. Above all, see how he consoles himself. Hadn't he expected someone to grieve with him and he didn't find him? To what consolation will he turn to someone who has been overcome by boredom because of sinners who forsook the law of God? Where will it go? To any man of God? Perhaps he had already experienced the great tribulation that exists in many of them, in whom he previously trusted greatly for some of their delight. From time to time one encounters just men and one rejoices with them, and it is necessary that one rejoices, because charity cannot exist without this joy; But, if something perverse occurs in those with whom man rejoiced, as often happens, the greater the joy was then, the greater the sadness is now, so that from now on man fears to let loose the reins of joy. He is already afraid to give himself over to joy, lest the happier he is, the more sad he will be if something adverse happens. Hurt, then, by the multitude of scandals, as by hic me occupavit, ut contra omnem consolationem clauderet mea is encouraged. Huic tali unde taedium? Fortasse quia vinea grandinata est, aut quia olea non provenit, aut quia vindemia a pluvia intercepta est. Unde huic taedium? Audi hoc ex alio psalmo. Ipsius enim et ibi vox est: Taedium detinuit me, a peccatorihus relinquentibus legem tuam (Ps 118,53). Tanto ergo taedio de huiusmodi malo affectum se iste dicit, ut denialet consolari anima ipsius. Prope absorbuerat eum taedium, tristitiaque eum omnino irreparabiliter merserat; Negat will console himself. Quid igitur restabat? 6 [v.4]. Primo vide unde consoletur. Nonne sustinuerat qui simul contristaretur, et non invenerat? (Ps 68,21). Quo enim se verteret ad consolationem, quem occupaverat taedium de peccatoribus relinquentibus legem Dei? 17 [v. l or j. You redeemed your people with your arm. With your arm, that is, with your power. And the arm of the Lord, to whom was it revealed? Maybe God put something there, whom we must look for with our hands at night so as not to deceive ourselves. Perhaps we are included in this distinction between the children of Israel and Joseph. By Joseph he wanted another town to be understood; the Gentile people. Why the Gentile people? Because Joseph was sold to Egypt by his brothers. That Joseph whom his brothers envied and for the same reason they sold him to Egypt, sold to Egypt, suffered and was humiliated, but, his innocence recognized, he was exalted, prospered and ruled. In all these things, what is symbolized? That? That Christ was also sold by his brothers and thrown out of his land as into the Egypt of the Gentiles. Sed quid fecit Deus? Notam fecisti in populis virtutem tuam. Inde congregationatio ista, Asaph transiliens, quia notam fecit in populis virtutem suam. Quam virtutem suam notam fecit in populis? 17 [v.16]. Redemisti in brachio tuo populum tuum. Brachio tuo: hoc est virtute tua. Et brachium Domini cui revelatum est? (Is 53,1). Redemisti in brachio tuo populum tuum, filios Israel, et loseph. You investigate the depth of the sea, what is deeper than human consciousness? This depth was troubled when God redeemed his people with his arm. When were the abysses disturbed? When, confessing all their consciences, they repented; and the abysses were troubled. 19 [v.18]. Great was the sound of the waters. In the praises of God, in the confession of sins, in the hymns, in the songs, in the prayers, the sound of the waters is immense. The clouds gave voices. Because the clouds shouted, this sound of the waters was produced, this disturbance of the abysses. What clouds are these? The preachers of truth. What clouds are these? Those with which God threatens a certain vineyard that produced thorns instead of grapes, saying: I will command my clouds not to rain water on it. So the apostles abandoned Ioseph populus ex Gentibus; Israel vero populus ex gente Hebraeorum. Redemit populum suum Deus, filios Israel et loseph. Why? Per lapidem angularem, in quo duo parietes copulati sunt (Eph 2,14). 18 [v.17]. Et exsequitur quomodo: Viderunt te aquae, Deus. Quid sunt aquae? Populi. Multitudo sonitus aquarum. In laudibus Dei, in confessionibus peccatorum, in hymnis et canticis, in orationibus, multitudo sonitus aquarum. Vocem dederunt clouds. Inde iste sonitus aquarum, inde abyssorum perturbatio, quia vocem dederunt clouds. What clouds? Praedicatores verbi veritatis. What clouds? Going to the Jews, they went to the Gentiles. The clouds shouted in all nations. Preaching Christ, the clouds cried out. 20 [v.19]. Your arrows actually passed. He calls their voices arrows. The words of the evangelists were the arrows. This is a similarity, because, properly speaking, neither the arrow is rain nor the rain an arrow; but, on the contrary, the word of God is an arrow because it wounds, and rain because it waters. No one, then, marveled at the disturbance of the abysses when the arrows passed. What does passed mean? They did not remain in the ears, but pierced the heart. The voice of your thunder in the wheel. As children we used to think that, when we heard thunder in the sky, it was like the noise of a cart leaving the stable; Therefore, thunder has a certain shaking similar to that of chariots. But do we have to think about these childish things again to understand what is said: the voice of your thunder in the wheel, as if God had some chariots in the clouds and their rolling produced that noise? There is no such thing. This is childish, vain and false. What does the voice of your thunder in the wheel mean? Let the voice roll. I don't understand it either. What will we do? We will question Iditho, for perhaps he will explain what he said: the voice of your thunder in the wheel. I don't understand; I will hear what you say: Your lightning flashed in the roundness of the earth. Say it, because I had not understood it. The orb of the earth is the wheel; for the circle of the earth's orb is rightly called roundness; hence the small wheel is also called a circle. The voice of your thunder in the wheel; they shone pluant super eam imbrem (Is v.6). Denique Apostoli telinquentes ludaeos, ierunt ad Gentes in ómnibus gentibus vocem dederunt clouds; Praedicating Christum, vocem dederunt clouds. 20 [v.19]. Etenim sagittae tuae pertransierunt. Easdem voices nubium rursus sagittas dixit. Verba enim Evangelistarum sagittae fuerunt. Similarities enim sunt. Nam proprie nec sagitta est pluvia, nec pluvia sagitta; at vero verbum Dei, et sagitta est, quia percutit, et pluvia, quia rigat. Nemo ergo iam miretur abyssorum conturbationem, quando sagittae tuae pertransierunt. Quid est, pertransierunt? Non in auribus remanserunt, sed corda transfixerunt. Vox tonitrui tui in broken. Quid est hoc? quomodo intellecturi sumus? Adiuvet Dominus. Vox tonitrui tui in broken.

Solebamus pueri suspicari, cum audiremus tonitrua de cáelo, quasi vehicula de stabulo processisse: habent enim tonitrua quamdam concussionem similem vehiculis. Numquid ad ista puerilia redituri sumus, ut intelligamus, Vox tonitrui tui in rota; quasi aliqua vehicula habeat Deus in nubibus, et transitus vehiculorum illum strepitum concitet? absit. Hoc puerile est, vanum, nugatorium. Quid est ergo, Vox tonitrui tui in rota? Return vox tua. Ñeque hoc intelligo. Quid faciemus? Interrogamus ipsum Idithun, ne forte ipse exponat quod dixit: Vox, inquit, tonitrui tui in rota. Non intelligo: audiam quid dicis: Apparuerunt fulgura tua orbi terrarum. Dec ergo: non intellexeram. your lightning in the roundness of the earth. Those clouds (the apostles) on the wheel, in the terrestrial circle, traveled around the globe of the earth, they traveled thundering and lightning; they moved the abysses; The precepts thundered and the lightning flashed. His voice resounded throughout the earth, and his words to the ends of the earth. The earth was moved and trembled, that is, all its inhabitants. They, by similarity, are the earth. Because? Because all people are included under the name of the sea, since human life is bitter and is subject to storms and storms. If you consider that men devour each other like fish, the larger swallowing the smaller, you will realize that the earth is this sea. The Evangelists walked there. 21 [v.20]. Your path is found in the sea. Before he said: Your way is in the Holy One. Now he says: Your way is in the sea, because the Holy One himself is in the sea and rightly walked on the waters of the sea. Your way is in the sea, that is, Christ is preached among the people. In another psalm it is said in this way: May God have mercy on us and bless us; Let your face be clear towards us so that we may know your way on earth. Where on earth? In all nations your Health. This is the same thing that now says: Your way is in the sea, and your paths in immense waters, that is, in many towns. And "your footprints are not known. I do not know to whom he refers when he says this, but I suspect that it is the Jews. Behold, the mercy of Christ has already been preached among the nations, in such a way that in the sea his way is found and his paths in immense waters, and, orbiculus appellatur. Vox tonitrui tui in rota: apparuerunt fulgura tua orbi terraram. Nubes illae in rota circumierunt orbem terrarum; terra. [v.20].

Iamdudum in Sancto via tua, moda in mari est via tua, quia ipse Sanctus in mari, et merit etiam super aquas maris ambulavit (Mt 14:25). In mari est via tua: id est in Gentibus praedicatur Christus tuus. In alio quippe psalmo ita dicitur: Deus misereatur nostri, et benedicat nos; illuminet vultum suum super nos, ut cognoscamus in terra viam tuam. Ubi in terra? In omnibus gentibus salutare tuum (Ps 66,2.3): hoc est, In mari est via tua. Et semitae tuae in aquis multis: hoc est, in populis multis. Et vestigia tua non cognoscentur. Nescio quos tetigit, et mirum nisi et ipsos Iudaeos. Ecce iam sic propalata est Gentibus misericordia Christi, ut in mari sit via tua, et semitae tuae in aquis multis; et vestigia tua non cognoscentur. Unde, a quibus

However, their traces are not known. Who ignores them? Those who still say: Christ has not yet come. Why do they say Christ has not come yet? Because they don't know that he walks on the sea. 22 [v.21]. You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. It's a bit difficult to figure out why he added this. Help us with your attention, because after these two verses the psalm and the sermon end, lest you, thinking that something else is missing, for fear of too much work or effort, pay little attention to what is present. Having said: Your way is in the sea, what we understand is in the people; and your paths in immense waters, that is, in many towns; He added: And your footprints are not known. We asked by whom they were ignored, and then he added: You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron, that is, your footprints are not known by the people who were led by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Why was this added if it wasn't to rebuke and reproach the reason for being in the sea? Why is his path in the sea if it is not because he was excluded from the land? They repudiated Christ; The sick did not want him to be their Savior, but he began to be the Savior of the Gentiles, of all nations, of immense peoples. However, the relics of his people were also saved. The ungrateful crowd was left out, for most of Jacob's thigh was limping. In the phrase the greater part of Jacob's thigh the multitude of the race is symbolized; And so it came to pass that the majority of the Israelites became a vain and foolish mob that did not know the footprints of Christ in the waters. Did you guide your people non cognoscentur, nisi ab his qui adhuc dicunt: Nondum venit Christus? Quare dicunt: Nondum venit Christus? Quia nondum agnoscunt super mare ambulantem. 22 [v.21]. Deduxisti sicut oves plebem tuam, in manu Moysi et Aaron. Quare hoc addiderit, indagare aliquantum difficile est. Adiuvate ergo nos intentione vestra, quia post ipsos duos versus finis erit, et Psalmi, et sermonis; ne forte cum aliquid restare arbitramini, timore laborís minus ad praesens attendatis. Cum dixisset, In mari est via tua, quod intelligimus, in gentibus; et semitae tuae in aquis multis, quod intelligimus, in populis multis, adiunxit: Et vestigia tua non agnoscentur.

Et quaerebamus a quibus non agnoscerentur; et subiecit continuo, Deduxisti sicut oves plebem tuam, in manu Moysi et Aaron: id est, ab ista plebe tua quae deducta est in manu Moysi et Aaron, vestigia tua non cognoscentur. Quare ergo positum est, nisi increpandi et exprobrandi causa, In mari est via tua? Unde in mari est via tua, nor even quia exclusa est a terra tua? Expulerunt Christum, noluerunt esse suum Salvatorem aegri: ille autem coepit esse in Gentibus, et in ómnibus gentibus, in multis populis. Salvae factae sunt etiam relice populi illius. Remansit foris ingrata multitudo, et claudicans lacob femoris latitudo (Gen 32,31). Latitudo cnim femoris intelligitur in multitudine generis, et facta est in maiori parte Israelitarum turba quaedam vana et insipiens, quae non agnosceret

like sheep, and did not know you. You gave them so many and such great goods! You divided the sea for them, you made them cross dry land in the middle of the waters, you submerged their enemy pursuers in the waves, you gave them manna in the desert, you led them by the hand of Moses and Aaron, and they rejected you so that your path would be in the sea and they would not know your footprints.

1 [v. l }. This Psalm contains the events that are narrated about the ancient people (of God). Through it, the new and subsequent people are warned to avoid being ungrateful for the benefits of God and to guard against arousing against themselves the wrath of Him from whom they must submissively and faithfully receive grace, so that they do not become, as the psalm says, like their fathers, a depraved and wrath-provoking generation; generation that did not straighten its heart, nor was its spirit faithful to God. This, then, is the desire of the psalm, this is the benefit, this is the most abundant fruit (which it intends to achieve). As all the things that are said and narrated in it appear clear and evident, its title asks and commands our attention in a special way. Not in vain is it titled: From intelligence to Asaf. Since we do not try to make known what sounds externally, but rather the internal meaning, that is why the things that are contained in it demand an intelligent understander. Next he has to narrate and remember things that seem to need a listener rather than an expositor. I will open my mouth in parables, he says; I will speak purposevestigia Christ! in here. Deduxisti sicut oves plebem tuam, et non te cognoverunt. So much cum illis bona fecisti! mare divisisti, inter aquas per aridam traiecisti, persequentes inimicos fluctibus operuisti, in deserto egenribus manila pluisti, deducens eos in mana Moysi et Aaron; er expulerunt te a se, ut in mari esset via tua, et vestigia tua non cognoícerent.

gifts from the beginning. Who doesn't shake laziness here? Who doesn't wake up from lethargy here? Who will dare to read in passing these parables and manifest propositions that by their very names indicate that it is advisable to study them in depth? The parable in itself contains the likeness of a thing; and although it is a Greek word, however, it is already used in Latin. And it is known that, in parables, the similarities of things that are narrated are compared with the things they are about. The propositions, which in Greek are called problemata, are questions that contain something that must be clarified through some explanation. Who will read parables and propositions lightly? Who, upon hearing them, will not pay attention to obtain their fruit by understanding? 2. Consider, my people, my law. Who are we to believe is speaking here if not God? He gave the law to his people, whom he gathered when they were delivered from Egypt. This congregation is properly called a synagogue, which means Asaph. Was Asaph understood because Asaph himself understood, or is it to be understood figuratively, because the synagogue himself understood, that is, the people, to whom it is said: Consider, my people, my law? But how is it that he rebukes the same people through the prophet, saying: Israel did not know me and my people did not understand me? However, there were among those people who, having faith, which was later revealed, not according to the letter of the law, but according to the grace of the spirit, understood. For those of their people who could foresee and prophesy the future manifestation of inquit, in parabolis os meum, eloquar propositiones ab initio were not without faith. Christ, when those ancient sacraments also symbolized the future ones. Or did only the prophets have this faith and the people lacked it? Rather, those who listened religiously to the prophets were helped by the same grace so that they understood what they heard. But, certainly, the secret of the kingdom of heaven was hidden in the Old Testament so that, in the fullness of time, it would be revealed in the New. The Apostle says: I do not want you, brothers, to be unaware that all our fathers were under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea, and that they were all baptized by Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and that they all ate the same spiritual food, and that they all drank the same spiritual drink, because they drank from the spiritual stone that followed them; and the stone was Christ. The same food and drink are found in their sacrament and in ours. But, if in meaning it is the same, in reality it is not, because the same Christ was given to them figured in the stone, and to us in the reality of the flesh. But God, says the Apostle, was not pleased with all of them. They all certainly ate the same spiritual food, and they all drank the same spiritual drink, that is, it meant something spiritual, but God was not pleased with all of them. By saying He was not pleased with all of them, there were undoubtedly some in whom God was pleased; Since all the sacraments were common, grace, which is the virtue of the sacrament, was not common to all. Just as now, once the faith that was then hidden has been revealed, the washing of regeneration, or baptism, is common in all those baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, but la fuerunt, qui eius in Christofuturam revelationem praevidere et praenuntiare potuerunt; cum et illa vetera sacramenta, significantia fuerintfuturum. However, neither then nor now is the voice of him who says, Consider, my people, my law fruitless. This word attendite, consider, was written like this in all the codices, since they do not say attend, consider, but attendite, consider. The people consist of many, to these many the following is said in plural: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth. It is the same thing to consider or heed that you incline your ear; and my law is also the same as the words of my mouth. Piously consider the law of God and the words of his mouth to whom humility inclines its ear, not to whom pride raises its neck or makes him proud. What is infused is received into the deep vessel of humility: what is thrown appears outside in the prominence of pride. Hence it is said in another place: Incline your ear and receive the words of understanding. Therefore, we are also sufficiently admonished to receive this psalm of understanding to Asaph with inclined ears, that is, with pious humility. I have recorded understanding for Asaph, because it was written in the title of the psalm intellectus, in the genitive, that is, of understanding and not the understanding. Nor was it said of Asaph, but for Asaph or to Asaph, as it appears in the Greek article to, which is also found in many Latin codices translated by ipsi, in the dative. These in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti baptizatis (Mt 28,19), common est lavacrum regenerationis; sed ipsa gratia cuius ipsa sunt Sacramenta, qua membra corporis Christi cum suo capite regenerata sunt, non communis est omnibus. Nam et haeretici habent eumdem Baptismum, et falsi fratres in communione catholici nominis. Ergo et hic recre dicitur: Sed non in ómnibus illis beneplacitum est Deo. 3- Ñeque tune tamen, ñeque never infructua est vox dicetis: Attendite, populus meus, legem meam.

All these things, being realities, happened to them in figure, and were written for our correction since it has come to fall upon us at the end of the ages. This was said with great precision and clarity to point out the grace of God, which not only works the remission of sins, but also makes the spirit of man cooperate in good work. By saying the above it is as if he were saying: his spirit did not believe God. To be the spirit faithful to God is not to believe that your spirit can work justice without God, but with God. This is also believing in God, which is undoubtedly more than believing in God. Likewise, many times you have to believe any man, even if you don't have to believe in the man. It could be judged that the works of the law were sufficient for justification, when those things that are commanded are executed outwardly by men who prefer not to be commanded the things that are not done from the heart and, nevertheless, are done; and for this reason it seems as if they walk in the law of God, but they do not want to walk, because they do not do it from the heart. In no way can what is done from the heart be done out of fear of punishment and not out of love for justice. When the plagues were spoken of in this psalm, what was stated about the evil angels is what we must not overlook: He sent the wrath of his indignation upon the Egyptians; the indignation, the anger, the tribulation, the message by the evil angels. No believer ignores that the devil and his angels exist, and so evil, certainly, that eternal fire is prepared for them. But that they, by ordering the Lord God, process messages to some, whom he deems worthy of this punishment, seems difficult to those who are incapable of thinking how the supreme justice of God uses well even the evil ones. As far as their nature or substance is concerned, who made them apart from Him? He did not create them evil, however, because he is good, he uses them well, that is, properly and fairly; just as, on the contrary, the wicked misuse their good creatures. Therefore non eodem ordine, decem tamen Aegyptiorum plaguee commemorantur; dum pro tribus quae sunt in Exodus (Ex 8,17; 9,10, et 10,22), et hic non sunt, id est, sciniphes, ulcera, tenebrae, aliae tres commemorantur quae ibi non sunt, id est, rubigo, pruina et ignis, non fulgurum, sed cui dicta est tradita possessio eorum, quod ibi non legitur. 28. But in these things the power of the good and bad angels is much greater, and, without a doubt, that of the good ones is greater; but whatever is permitted and ordered by the will of God; the same as us too. Then this man of God also tells God what he learned from God, as a disciple who speaks to the teacher, who does not ignore, but judges; and, therefore, he speaks either to the one who approves what he taught, or to the one who reviles what he did not teach; especially taking into account that the prophet personifies in himself, in the figure of a petitioner, those who will exist when these coming things happen. Before saying this, the Apostle had commemorated the prophetic oracle about the future disbelief of the people of Israel: All day I stretched out my hands to the people who did not believe and who contradicted. So, so that no one, misunderstanding, would think that all the people, for the crime of disbelief and opposition to God, had been condemned, he added next: Well, I tell you: did God reject his people? Here he shows which people he referred to; without a doubt to the first people, since, if God had reproved and condemned all the people, he would certainly not be an apostle of Jesus Christ, being as he was an Israelite of the race of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. He also quotes the extremely convenient testimony of Elijah when he says: Do you not know what the Scripture says through the mouth of the prophet Elijah? How he goes to God against Israel, and says: Lord, they killed your prophets, they undermined the altars, and I am left alone and they intend to take my life. But what does the divine oracle answer? Likewise, he also said in another circumstance: I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them so that there may be one flock and one shepherd, pointing out the Gentiles that he was to attract to himself, not personally, so that in this way what he said would be true: I have not been sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, but for his Gospel, which were to spread the beautiful feet of those who announce peace, of those who announce good things. After this inheritance we must take what is sung in the prophecy of this psalm: O God, the nations came to your inheritance, in such a way that we understand that the people came to the Church not believing, but persecuting, that is, that they broke into it with the desire to destroy and annihilate it completely, as demonstrated by such a great number of persecutions. It is important to understand what follows: They profaned your holy temple, as if executed, not in the works of wood or in the works of stone, but in the men of whom the apostle Saint Peter says that the house of God is built as living stones. Hence the apostle Saint Paul also clearly says: You are the temple of God. Thus, then, the persecutors certainly desecrated this temple in those whom they forced, by terrifying and tormenting, to deny "Gentes autem super misericordia glorificare Deum": ecce quod est, "Habeo alias oves quae non sunt de hoc ovili; oportet me et ipsas adducere, ut sit unus grex et unus pastor." always? as if it were said, do not be angry, Lord, forever. Also in what follows: Your indignation will burn like fire, it must be understood how long and forever as if it were said: How long will your indignation burn like fire forever? Well, here these two expressions must be understood as above, when saying only once: they gave for food, and it was also understood as said in the second sentence. The first sentence says: They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the air. This word was missing in the following sentence, which says: The flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth, but it is understood, what was recorded in the previous sentence, they gave. The expressions of anger and jealousy, or indignation of God, are not disturbances of God, as some who do not understand the holy Scriptures maintain; but, under the name of anger, is understood the punishment of iniquity, and, under the name of zeal, or indignation, the demand for purity of customs, so that the soul may not despise the Law of its Lord and, for worshiping its God, perish. These impulses or movements, due to the effect, are turbulent in the affliction of men, but they are calm in the disposition of God, to whom it was said: You, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility. These words sufficiently demonstrate that these tribulations occur because of the sins of men, even if they are faithful, even though from here the glory of the martyrs shines by virtue of patience and the conduct of instruction in the punishment of the Lord is preserved with piety. This is confirmed by the Maccabees in the midst of cruelest torments, this is witnessed by the three young men in the midst of the harmless flames, this is confirmed by the holy prophets in captivity. Even when dictum is, here it saysretur, Noli, Domine, irasci in finem. Nam ita hic duo ista subaudienda sunt, sicut superius unum illud quod dictum esr, posuerunt: nam cum habeat prior sententia, Posuerunt morticina servorum tuorum escás volatilibus caeli, hoc verbum posterior non habet, ubi dictum est, Carnes sanctorum tuorum bestiis terrae; sed subauditur utique quod habet superior, posuerunt. Ira porro et zelus Dei, non sunt perturbationes Dei, sicut nonnulli Scripturas quas non intelligunt argument: sed nomine irae intelligitur vindicta iniquitatis; nomine zeli exactio castitatis, ne anima legem Domini sui contemnat, et a Deo suo fornicando dispereat. Then how is one to understand what the Lord says in the Gospel: The servant who did not know the will of his master, and does things worthy of punishment, will be beaten with few; But the servant who knew the will of his master, and performs works worthy of punishment, will be beaten with many, if the wrath of God is greater on the nations that do not know the Lord? for he says: Return to our neighbors seven times more. Or will this happen because there is a great difference between the servants who, even though they ignore the will of their master, nevertheless invoke his name, and the strangers to the great father of the family, who so ignore the Lord that they do not invoke God? For, instead of knowing Him, they invoke idols, demons or any creature, and not the Creator blessed forever and ever. To these of whom he prophesies this, he does not declare them so ignorant of the will of their Lord* that they still fear the Lord; but they are so ignorant of the Lord that they do not call upon him and, furthermore, they are enemies of his name. Therefore there is a great difference between the servants who ignore the will of their Lord and yet live in their family and in their house, and the enemies, who not only do not want to know their Lord, but also do not call on his name and, furthermore, attack their servants.

Where does some bond of greed hold you back that prevents you from loving God; and see if it is not that which created the one whom you despise. Why do you love these things if it's not because they are beautiful? But can they be as beautiful as the one who created them? You admire these things because you don't see Him; love those you don't see for the things you see. Ask the creature. If it exists by itself, it remains in itself. If it is made by Him, it is only harmful to her lover because He puts her before the Creator. Why have I said this? For this little verse, my brothers. Those who loved God only so that it might go well with them in the flesh were dead; for the mind according to the flesh is death; and dead are those whom God does not love freely, that is, because He is good, not because He gives us such goods as He also gives to the bad. 1 [v. l]. It is my responsibility to speak to you about this psalm. Your silence helps my voice, since sometimes it weakens. The attention of the listeners and the mandate of those who order me will give me the strength to speak. The title of the psalm reads: For the end in favor of the winepresses, in the fifth fair. Psalm for Asaph. Many mysteries are accumulated in a single title; and in such a way that the cover or frontispiece of the psalm indicates what is contained in it. When talking about the winepresses, none of you expect that I will have to explain anything about the basin, the press, the beam and the baskets; since the psalm does not speak of them either and, for the same reason, it rather foreshadows a mystery. If the text of the psalm contained something similar, there would be those who would judge that the winepresses should be taken literally, and that nothing more should be sought and that nothing was recorded in a mystical sense meaning something sacred; But I would say that the psalm speaks briefly about the winepresses and you want to induce me to think I don't know what. When the psalm was read you heard nothing about the winepresses. Then take the winepresses as a sacrament of the Church, which is now discussed. In the winepresses we notice three things: the tamping; and two others are derived from it: one, which is collected; another, which is thrown. In the PSALMUS

S ERMO 1 [v.l]. Loqui ad vos de praesenti psalmo suscepimus: adiuvet vocem nostram quies vestra; etenim aliquanto est obtunsior: dabit ei vires intentio audientium, et adiutorium iubentis ut loquar. Titulum habet psalmus iste: In jinem pro torcularibus, quinta sabbati, Psalmus ipsi Asapb. In unum titulum fines sunt congesta mysteria; ita tamen ut limen Psalmi indicet interiora. Cum de torcularibus locuturi sumus, nemo vestrum aliquid exspeetet nos dicturos esse de lacu, de prelo, de fiscinis; quia nec ipse psalmus hoc habet, et ideo magis indicat mysterium. Nam et si aliquid tale Psalmi textus contineret, non deesset qui putaret ad litteram esse accipienda torcularia, nec aliquid illic amplius requirendum, nec mystice aliquid positum, et sacrate significatum; sed diceret: Simpliciter Psalmus de torcularibus loquitur, et tu mihi nescio quid aliud suspicaris. Nihil hic tale audistis, cum legeretur. Ergo accipite torcularia mysterium Ecclesiae, quod nunc agitur. In torcularibus animadvertimus quaedam tria: pressuram, et de pressura quaedam duo; unum recondendum, alterum proíícíendum. Fít ergo in torculari conculcado, tribu latio, pondus: et in his oleum eliquatur occulte in gemellarium; public amurca

per stalls currit. Intendite ad magnum hoc spectaculum. Non enim desinit Deus edere nobis quod cum magno gaudio spectemus: aut circi insania huic spectaculo comparaanda est? Quando ergo auditis contumaciter garriré blasphemos, et dicere, abundare pressuras temporibus christianis; scitis enim quia hoc amant dicere: et vetus quidem, sed a temporibus christianis coepit proverbium, Non pluit Deus, duc ad Christianos. The psaltery and the zither consist of the fact that the psaltery is made of wood with a concavity placed in the upper part, in which the strings vibrate and sound; These are pressed at the bottom and sound at the top. When he has believed, when he has been baptized, when he has begun to embark on the path of God, when he has prepared himself to be liquefied in the oil mill and has clearly separated himself from the dregs, he will have many persecutors, many insulters, many detractors, many who dissuade and threaten as they can, terrifying and depressing: all this is the water of contradiction. That's how I think it's happening here today, because I think there are many who their friends tried to drag to the circus and I don't know what frivolities of today's festivity; but perhaps the former led the latter to the church. Well, whether they attracted them, or whether they could not have been dragged to the circus by them, the truth is that they were tested in the water of contradiction. He declares to which gods he refers and in what congregation God is found, when he says: I said, you are gods, and all sons of the Most High. However, you, as men, will die, and fall like one of the princes. Then God stood in the middle of the synagogue or congregation of those children of the Most High, of whom the Most High himself says through Isaiah: I created and magnified the children, but they despised them. We take the people of Israel as a synagogue, because that is what it is usually called properly, although it is also called the Church. The apostles never called our people or congregation a synagogue, but always Church; either to distinguish it, or because there is some difference between the word congregation, from which the synagogue took its name; and convocation, from where the Church took it. Gather is usually applied to beasts, and therefore the word gather more appropriately indicates what is most appropriate, that is, to flocks; and summoning applies rather to those who are endowed with reason, that is, to men. Hence in another psalm it is sung in the person of Asaph: I became like a donkey with you, and I am always with you. This was certainly said when, although he appeared to be given to one God, he tried to obtain from Him, as a great and supreme thing, temporal carnal and earthly goods. However, we often see that they are called children, not by the grace that belongs to the New Testament, but by that which belongs to the Old; since by this grace he chose Abraham, of whose flesh he formed the great people, and by it he also loved Jacob, while he was not yet born, and hated Esau; by the same he brought out the people among the Egyptians and introduced them, haidem iste psalmus asserat, et quos déos intelligi velit, in quorum synagoga stetit Deus, apertius exprimat, ubi ait: Ego dixi, Dii estis, et fiüi Altissimi omnes; vos autem sicut homines moriemini, et sicut unus de principibus cadetis. In horum ergo synagoga filiorum Altissimi, de quibus idem Altissimus per Isaiam dicit, Filios genui et exaltavi; ipsi autem me spreverunt (Is 1,2), stetit Deus. Nostram vero Apostoli nunquam synagogam dixerunt, sed semper Ecclesiam; sive discernendi causa, sive quod inter congregationem unde Synagoga, et convocationem unde Ecclesia nomen accepit, distet aliquid; quod scilicet congregari et pécora solent, atque ipsa proprie, quorum et greges proprie dicimus; summon autem magis est utentium ratione, sicut sunt homines. Unde ex persona ipsius Asaph in alio psalmo canitur, Quasi pecus factus sum apud te, et ego semper tecum (Ps 72,23): quando utique, quamvis uni vero Deo mancipatus videretur, pro magnis tamen ac summis bonis ab illo carnalia, terrena, temporalia requirebat. Invenimus eos saepe etiam filios appellatos; non ea gratia quae ad Novum Testamentum pertinet, sed illa quae ad Vetus: quia et ipsa gratia est qua elegit Abraham, et ex eius carne tam magnum populum propagavit; qua nondum natos, lacob dilexit. Next we must investigate whether we should understand that the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself was placed in the same synagogue of the gods to judge among them; because each person in and of himself is God, and the Trinity itself is one God. It is not an easy question to elucidate, because it cannot be denied that God is present in all things created by the presence, not corporal, but spiritual, according to its substance, in an admirable way and barely intelligible to few, and to which it is said: If I ascend to heaven, there you are; If I go down to hell, you are present. Therefore, it is rightly demonstrated that God is invisibly found in the congregation of men, since He fills heaven and earth, as the prophet Jeremiah announces about Him; and it is not only demonstrated, but, according to the reach of the human mind, it is somehow known that it is found in the things that it created if, in turn, the man is next to it and hears it, and is rejoiced with great joy by the eternal voice of the bridegroom. However, as far as I believe, this psalm is ready to declare something that was done from a certain time here so that God would be found in the middle of the synagogue of the gods; because that permanence by which it fills heaven and earth, neither pro-

piously belongs to the synagogue, nor does it change over time. Consequently, God placed himself in the synagogue of the gods; but he who said of himself, I was not sent except to the sheep that perished of the house of Israel. The reason is also said: To judge among the gods. I acknowledge, therefore, that God was found in the midst of the synagogue of the gods; of those whose parents are the same from whom Christ descends according to the flesh. That God might be in the midst of the synagogue of the gods, he proceeded from them according to the flesh. But what is this God? It is not who are those in whose synagogue it was found, but as the Apostle declares where he wrote: That he is the God above all things, worthy to be blessed forever. I recognize that it was found there; I recognize that the husband God was found in the midst, of whom a certain friend of his says: In your midst is he whom you do not know; since it is said of them shortly after in this psalm: They did not know, nor did they understand; They walk in darkness. The Apostle himself also attests to this when he says: For blindness came in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations had entered. Being in their midst, they saw him, but they did not see him as God, as he wanted them to see him, as he says: He who sees me sees my Father. He separates the gods, not by virtue of their merits, but by their grace, since from the same batch or dough he makes some vessels for honor, and others for contumelia. Who is it that separates you? 1 [v.l]. The title of this psalm is: Psalm Song for Asaph. I have said many times that Asaph means congregation or gathering. Proinde ut hoc vitium sanetur, ex ipsius prophetae persona dicitur: Surge, Deus, indica terram. Tumuit enim terra, cum te crucifigeret, emerge a mortuis, et judica terram. Quoniam tu disperses in omnibus gentibus: quid, nisi terram? hoc est, eos qui terrena sapiunt; sive ipsum affectum in credentibus terrenae cupiditatis et elationem absumens; sive non credentes, terram conterendam, perdendamque discernens. Sic per membra sua, quorum conversatio in caelis est, iudicat terram, et disperse in omnibus gentibus. Nec praetereundum, quod nonnulli codices habent, Quoniam tu haereditabis in omnibus gentibus: quia et hoc non inconvenient accipitur, ñeque ut simul utrumque sit quidquam repugnar. congregation of God's people, appears in the titles of many psalms. Congregation, in Greek, is called synagogue. This was like the proper name of the Jewish people, since it was called a synagogue; just as the Christian people are commonly called the Church, despite also being a congregation. 2 [v.2]. The people of God say, then, in this psalm: 'O God,' who will be like you? This, I believe, should be more appropriately applied to Christ, because, being made in the likeness of men, it was judged by those who despised him that he should be compared to other men. He was also counted among the wicked, but this when he was judged. When he comes as a judge to judge, then what is said here will be fulfilled: O God, who will be like you? If the psalms did not usually speak of Christ, what no faithful person can doubt was said to him would not be said: Your throne, O God!, forever and ever; scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom, you loved justice and hated iniquity; That is why, O God, your God anointed you with the oil of joy on your companions. Now to him it is said: O God, who will be like you? You wanted to be similar in contempt to many, even similar to the thieves who were crucified with you. But when you come in majesty: Who will be like you? What extraordinary thing is said when it is said to God: Who will be like you, if this is not said to Him in that He wanted to be like men by taking the form of a man and being made in the likeness of men, and found in clothing like a man? That is why it is not added here, who is like you?, which would no doubt rightly be said si esto morum titulis ponitur. Graece autem congregationtio synagoga dicitur, quod velut proprium nornen Iudaeorum populus tenuit, ut Synagoga appellaretur; sicut populus Christianus usitatius vocatur Ecclesia, cum et ipse utique congregetur. 2 [v.2]. Populus ¡taque Dei in isto psalmo dicit: Deus, quis similis erit tibi? Quod ego arbitrar accommodatius accipi in Christo, quia in similaireine hominum factus, putatus est ab eis a quibus contemptus est, caeteris hominibus compatandus: nam et inter iniquos deputatus est (Is 53:12); sed ad hoc ut iudicaretur. Cum autem veniet iudicaturus, tune fiet quod hic dicitur, Deus, quis similis erit tibi?

Si enim Psalmi non solerent loqui ad Dominum Christum, non dicetetur etiam illud, quod ipsi dictum esse nullus potest dubitare fidelium: "Thronus tuus, Deus, in saeculum saeculi, virga directionis, virga regni tui: dilexisti iustitiam, et odisti iniquitatem; propterea unxit te, Deus, Deus tuus oleo exsultationis prae participibus tuis" (Ps 44,7.8). Huic ergo et nunc dicitur, Deus, quis similis erit tibi? Multis enim similis in humilitate esse voluisti, usque et latronibus qui tecum sunt crucifixi (Luke 23,33); sed in claritate cum venies, quis similis erit tibi? Quid enim magnum dicitur, cum Deo dicitur, Quis similis erit tibi; nisi illi dicatur, qui similis esse hominibus voluit formam serví accipiens, in similarityine hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut homo? Therefore, continue: Do not be silent or restrain yourself, O God! He says this because he first remained silent to be judged when, like a lamb before the shearer, he was silent, not opening his mouth and thus repressing his power. To demonstrate that he had repressed him, we see how, at the voice by which he said I am, those who were looking for him to arrest him retreated and fell to the ground. How would He be captured and suffer if He had not been contained and repressed and in a certain way calmed down? In such a way that some interpreted what was recorded here: Do not contain yourself, O God!, that they translated it as: Do not calm yourself, O God! He himself says in another place: He was silent; But do I always have to be silent? To him who is told here: Do not be silent, in another place it is said of him: God will clearly come; our God, and will not be silent. Here it is said: Don't be silent. He was silent, therefore, when he came undercover to be judged; However, he will not be silent when he clearly comes to judge. 3 [v.3]. Behold, your enemies stirred up, and those who hated you lifted up their heads. It seems to me that in this the last times are announced when these voices, which are now repressed by fear, have to break out freely, but irrationally, so that they have to be called noise or sound rather than locution or speech. They will not begin to hate then, but then those who hated you will raise their heads; not the heads, but the head, when they must reach such a level that, having as their head the one who is exalted above all that is

For they deliberated unanimously, and together established a covenant or testament against You, as if they could be stronger (than You). In Holy Scripture, a will is not only called a document that only has value after the death of the testator, but rather every pact, agreement or contract. Thus Laban and Jacob stipulated a will, which also had value inter vivos. In the Holy Scripture there are countless similar covenants. 7 [v.7.8]. He then begins to enumerate the enemies of Christ under certain Gentile names; and the meaning of the names sufficiently makes known what is meant. Congruently, the enemies of the truth are symbolized in such names. The name Idumeans means bloodthirsty or earthly. That of Ishmaelites, those who obey themselves, not God. The one from Moab, the one that comes from the father. This is by no means understood more aptly in a bad sense; taking into account the same story, since Father Lot begat him from the illicit union that his daughter had with him, from which fact he took this name. In a good sense he would be a good father, but if someone uses the law legitimately, not illicitly and incestuously. The name Hagarenes means proselytes, that is, upstarts. Under this name are symbolized the enemies of the people of God, not those who become citizens, but those who with a spurious and adventitious spirit persevere as citizens, who are mahae, cui dicit Apostolus, Ergo Abrahae semen estis, secundum promissionem. haeredes (Gal 3:29): non Israel secundum carnem, de quo dicit, Videte Israel secundum carnem (1 Cor 10:18). 6 [v.6]. The name aliens, according to the Latin word, means foreigners, and, therefore, enemies; In Hebrew, however, they are called Philistines, which is translated as those who fall due to drink, such as those who have been intoxicated by the lust of the world. The name of Tyre, in the Hebrew language, is called Sor, which is translated as anguish or tribulation, and according to this, what the Apostle says must be taken regarding these enemies of the people of God: The Lord will give tribulation and anguish to every soul of man who works evil. All of these are thus enumerated in this psalm: The tents of the Idumeans, and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalee, and the foreigners (the Philistines) with the inhabitants of Tyre. 8 [v. 9]. Indicating the cause of why they are enemies of God's people, he adds and says: Since Ashur came with them. Assur is usually figuratively symbolized by the devil, who works in the children of disbelief as his instruments to combat the people of God. They joined together to help the children of Lot, because all the enemies, their prince the devil acting on them, confederated to lend their help to the children of Lot: which is translated as the one who deviates or goes astray. The prevaricating angels very well symbolize the children of digression, since, departing from the truth, they became satellites of the devil. These are those of whom the Apostle says: It is not se ostendunt. Gebal, Vallis vana, id est, fallaciter humilis: Amon, Populus turbidus, vel Populus moeroris: Amalech, Populus lingens; unde alibi dictum est, Et inimici eius terram lingent (Ps 71,9). Alienigenae, quamvis et ipso nomine latino se indicent alienos, et ob hoc consequenter inimicos, tamen in hebraeo dicuntur Philistiim; quod interpretatur Cadentes potione, -velut quos fecit ebrios luxuria saecularis. Tyrus lingua hebraea dicitur Sor; quod sive Angustia sive Tribulatio interpretetur, secundum illud accipiendum est in his inimicis populi Dei, quod ait Apostolus: Tribulatio et anguish in omnem animam hominis operantis malum (Rom 2,9).

Let us now see what the prophetic spirit imprecates, predicting rather than cursing: Do with them what you did with Midian and Sisera, or what you did with Jabin in the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor and became like dung of the earth. The people of Israel, who were then the people of God, defeated and subdued all of these, as history attests; the same as those whom he then commemorates by saying: He treats his leaders like Oreb and Zeb, and Zebek and Sálmana. The meaning of these names is the following: Midian means he who turns away judgment; Sisera, exclusion from joy; and Jabin, wise. But in these enemies of the people of God, the wise man must be understood as the one of whom the Apostle says: Where is the wise man? Where is the lawyer? Where is the persecutor of this century? Oreb means dryness; Zeb, wolf; Zebec, victim, but of the wolf, since he has his own victims. Sálmana, shadow of restlessness. All these names are appropriate for the evil ones, whom the people of God defeat with good. Finally, Kishon, in whose torrent they were defeated, means their hardness. And Endor, where they perished, means source of generation, but carnal. Coming to this confession, they will be so confused that they will please; and in such a way they will perish, that they will remain. Know, he says, that your name is Lord. 1 [v. l]. This psalm is titled in favor of the winepresses. And as your charity points out to me, since I notice that you are listening with great interest, there was no mention at all about the press, or the sieve, or the pilón, or the containers, or the winepress building. We have heard nothing at all about such things in him. Then from here a big question arises: What does the title that says: In favor of the winepresses mean? Certainly, if after the title he had mentioned any of the things that I commemorated, one could believe for the carnal that he undoubtedly wanted to celebrate these material winepresses. But since it was titled in favor of the winepresses and no verse of the psalm later spoke of these winepresses that are very well known to the human eye, there is no doubt that they are other winepresses that the Spirit of God wanted to be here omnem terram; utique et in omni cáelo, vel super hear me caelum: sed hoc dicere maluit, quo terrena superbia premeretur. Desinit enim superbire terra, id est homo, cui dictum est, Terra es (Gen 3,19); et, Quid superbit terra et cinis? (Eccli 10,9) cum cognoscit Dominum esse altissimum super omnem terram, id est, nullius hominis cogitationes valere adversus eos qui secundum propositum vocati sunt, et de quibus dicitur, Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? (Rom 8,28.31). PSALMUS

1 [v. l]. Psalmus iste, Pro torcularibus, inscribitur. Et quantum advertit nobiscum Charitas Vestra (quia vos intentissime audire advertebamus), nihil in eius textu dictum est vel de prelo, vel de fiscinis, vel de lacu, vel de instrumentis aut aedificio torcularis; omnino nihil in eo tale audimus: unde quid sibi velit titulus eius, quod inscribitur, Pro torcularibus, non parva quaestio est. Profecto enim si post istum titulum aliquid de talibus rebus diceret, quales commemoravi, crederetur a carnalibus veré ista visibilia torculada voluisse cantore: quia vero titulum imposuit, Pro torcularibus, et nihil postea in omni versu Psalmi dixit de his torcularibus notissimis oculis nostris; non dubitatur esse allia torcularia quae nos hic quaerere et intelligere voluit Spiritus Dei. understood and investigated. Therefore, let us remember what is done in these visible winepresses, and thus we will understand how spiritual work is done in the Church. The grape certainly hangs on the vine, and the olive on the olive tree. Wine presses are usually used for these two types of fruits; While they hang like fruits, they freely enjoy the air; and the grape is not wine nor the olive oil before tamping. Such are the men whom God predestined before the age of the century to make them like the image of his only begotten Son, who in a special way was squeezed like a great bunch of grapes. Then in this way men, before approaching the service of God, enjoy in the century as if a delicious freedom, in the style of the grape and the olive that hang from the vine and the olive tree. But as it was written: Son, when you approach the service of God, remain in righteousness and fear and prepare your soul for temptation; When someone approaches the service of the Lord, let him recognize that he has entered the winepress; He will therefore be troubled, broken, compressed; not to perish in this world, but to flow into liquid form into the cellars of the Lord. It strips away the wrappings of carnal desires as well as the pomace. This happens with carnal desires, for which the Apostle says: Put off the old man and put on the new. This is not completely done if it is not through tribulations; hence there are ominous winepresses of the Church of God of the present time. 2. But who of us are placed in the winepresses? The sons of Korah. Therefore it was added: E » favor of the wine presses for the sons of Korah. From what those who, knowing agatur in his visibilibus torcularibus recordemur, et hoc videamus quemadmodum spiritualiter geratur in Ecclesia, could clarify for us. Uva certe pendet in vitibus, et oliva in arboribus (his enim duobus fructibus solent torcularia praeparari); et quamdiu pendent in fruticibus suis, tanquam libero aere perfruuntur; et nec uva vinum est, nec oliva oleum, ante pressuram.
