All those who call themselves blessed on earth possess something and perform something. He who owns many estates, much servants, much gold and silver is called blessed. Possessing this he is called blessed. He who achieved certain honors is also said to be blessed: the consulate, the prefecture. Acting in this is called blessed. Then they are called blessed or possessing or acting. But how are they to be blessed there (in that house)? Where should they live? What are they to do? I already said where they should live. Blessed are those who dwell in your house. You, if you had your own house, you are poor; If you had God's, you are rich. In your house you will fear thieves; God is the impassable wall of your house. Therefore blessed are those who live in your house. Everyone possesses the heavenly Jerusalem without narrowness, without oppression, without diversity and division of boundaries; everyone possesses it and each one possesses it completely. Its riches are immense. There brother does not shake brother; there is no poverty there. What should they do there? The mother of all human actions is necessity. I have said it, brothers, briefly. Go through any kind of actions with your thoughts, and observe that only necessity engenders them. The same arts that protect eloquence and defend medicine, which manifest themselves excellently in helping, are excellent actions in this world. Make the litigants disappear: who will the lawyer defend? Wounds and diseases disappear: what will the doctor cure? Likewise, all the operations that daily life demands and executes arise from necessity.

Plow, sow, plant a vineyard, sail; All these works, who generates them but necessity and poverty? It nullifies hunger, thirst, nakedness; What need will there then be for these works? These works that are commanded to us are good, because all those that I commemorated are decent to all men; and understand that I am not talking about the terrible and detestable works: of infamies and crimes, of homicides, of theft, of adulteries, because I do not count these things among human actions; Of the honest ones that I speak of, they are only engendered by the need for the weakness of the flesh. Well, those that I said are recommended to us: Break your bread with the hungry, with whom will you break it where there is no one who feels hungry? Receive the poor and homeless in your house, what pilgrim should you receive there where everyone lives in their homeland? Which sick person should you visit where they enjoy perfect health? Which litigant will you agree with where peace is eternal? What dead person must you bury there where people always live? You must perform none of those works plausible to men; You must do none of these good works, because the turtledove's chicks have already flown from the nest. So what? You already said where we should live: Blessed are those who live in your house. Tell us what to do, because I don't see any need there that impels me to act. See that necessity now engenders what I speak and expound. Is there perhaps such an exhibition there to teach these things to the ignorant and remind the forgetful? Listen to this lagareña struggle from the lips of the apostle Saint Paul, because he too was crushed here, he was pressed: I take pleasure, he says, in the law of God, according to the inner man; But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and holding me captive to the law of sin, which is in my members. Great struggle and great distress to avoid it, unless help comes immediately. Unhappy man I, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Then he also in this psalm saw those joys and said in his heart: Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord!; forever and ever they will praise you. But who will go up there? What will I do about the weight of the meat? Blessed are those who live in your house; forever and ever they will praise you. I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. but, when the command came, sin revived, says the Apostle; but I am dead. The law was given to men, not to save them, but so that they would know by it what illness they were in. Hear the words of the Apostle: If the law had been given that could give life, then justice would be due at all to the law. But the Scripture enclosed everything under sin so that the promise could be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ. So that, when grace came after the law, it found the man, not only prostrate, but also confessing and saying: Wretched man I, who will deliver me from this body of death? And so opportunely the doctor came to the valley of tears and said: Truly you knew that you fell; Hear me so you can get up, you who fell because you despised me. Therefore, the law was given to convince the sick with illness, who believed himself to be healthy: to clarify sins, not to erase them. Since sin was made evident by the law that was given, sin increased, because sin is opposed to the law; For thus says the Apostle: Taking advantage of the opportunity, sin, gaining momentum through the law, worked all covetousness in me. What does it mean to have taken advantage of the opportunity by law? That having received the mandate, men tried to act as if with their own strength, and, overcome by greed, they became guilty of transgressing the same mandate. But what does the Apostle say? Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more; That is, the disease increased, the medicine was provided. Therefore, brothers, did those five porticos of Solomon that surrounded the pool, and in which the sick lay, heal the sick? We read in the Gospel that the sick lay in the five porches. Aque remus mandatum; adveniente autem command, peccatum revixit: ego autem mortuus sura; hoc ait Apostolus. ethically when these psalms were originally sung and written. For the rest, as far as this time is concerned, the Lord has already shown his mercy to the nations and granted them his salvation. But as he heals the eyes of the heart so that it can be seen, for the same reason, after having said: Show us your mercy, as if he had said it to many blind people who were going to say, How will we see when he begins to show it?, he added and give us your health. Giving his health heals in us that by which we can see what he makes known. He does not cure like the male doctor, in order to show this light to those he has cured. This light that must be made to see is one thing, and the same doctor who heals the eyes, to whom he manifests this light, whose light he is not himself, is another. The Lord our God does not act like this. He himself is the doctor, who heals so that we can see and the light that we can see. However, let us carefully review, as much as we can, as much as the Lord grants us and as the scarcity of time allows, briefly, the entire psalm. 2 [v. l]. Its title is: For the end; Psalm for the sons of Korah. Let us only understand the end of that of which the Apostle says: The end of the law is Christ in order to justice for every believer. Then, by first recording in the title of the psalm for the end, he directed our hearts toward Christ. If we head towards him, we will not err, because he is the truth towards which we walk quickly; and he is the path where we run. What in prophetia, cum primum Psalmi isti dicerentur et scriberentur: caeterum quod attinet ad hoc tempus, iam ostendit Dominus Gentibus misericordiam suam, et dedit eis salutare suum. Ule quidem ostendit; sed multi sanari nolunt, ut videant quod otendit. Sed quia ipse sanat oculos cordis ad videndum se; propterea cum dixisset, Ostende nobis misericordiam tuam, tanquam multis caecis dicturis, Quomodo videbimus, cum coeperit ostendere? adiunxit, Et salutare tuum da nobis.

Dando enim salutare suum, sanat in nobis unde possimus videre quod otendit: non quomodo medicas homo ipse curat, ut luzem istam ostendat eis quos curaverit; et aliud est ista lux quam demonstraturus est, aliud autem ipse medicus qui curat oculos quibus ostendat luzm, quae lux non est ipse. Non ergo sic Dominus Deus noster: ipse est enim medicus qui curat unde videre possimus, et ipse est lux quam videre possimus. Totum tamen Psalmum breviter, quantum possumus, quantum donat Dominus, pro anguish temporis attenti curramus. 2 [v. l]. Titulus eius est, In finem, filiis Core, Psalmus. Finem non inteliigamus, nisi quem dicit Apostolus, Finís enim Legis Christus, ad iustitiam omni credenti (Rom 10:4). Ergo cum primo in titulo Psalmi posit, In finem; direxit cor nostrum in Christum. In illum si intendamus, non errabimus; quia ipse est veritas quo festinamus, et ipse est via per quam curramus (lo 14,6). What is it, Filiis Core? Interpretatur Core ex Hebrew verb in Latinum Calvus. Ergo filiis Core, filiis calvi. Quis est ist S-Ag. 21

What does it mean for the sons of Korah? The Hebrew word Korah is translated into Latin as calvus, the bald one. Therefore for the sons of Korah it is the same as for the sons of the bald man. Who is this bald guy? Bald, not so that we laugh at him, but so that we cry before him. Certain individuals laughed and were devastated by demons; just as it is told in the books of the Kings that certain children laughed at the bald Elysium saying behind their backs: Bald, bald, and when bears came out of the forest, they devoured them and were mourned by their parents. This fact prophetically symbolized our Lord Jesus Christ; for he was mocked as bald by the Jewish mockers, since he was crucified in the place of the skull. On the contrary, we, if we had believed in him, are his children. To us, then, this psalm is sung when it says: For the sons of Korah, for we are the sons of the bridegroom. In fact, the husband, giving the pledge to his wife, his blood and the Holy Spirit, with which he enriched us while we are on this pilgrimage, still reserves for us his hidden riches. He who gave such garments, what does he reserve? 3 [v. 2]. The prophet sings it in the future tense, but uses the past tense, narrating what is going to happen as happened, because for God what is going to happen has already happened. Then in prophecy the prophet saw what was to happen to us as happening in the providence and predestination of God; to the same thing that says in that psalm, in which everyone recognizes Christ, because it is recited in such a way that it seems the Gospel is read: They pierced my hands and feet, they counted all my bones, but they observed me and looked; and they divided my garments among themselves, and

They cast lots for my tunic. Who, upon hearing the reader read the psalm, does not recognize the Gospel? And yet, when expressing this in the psalm, it was not said that they should pierce my hands and feet, but rather pierce my hands and my feet; nor was it said that my bones should be counted, but rather they counted my bones; nor was it said that they should divide my garments, but rather they divided my garments among themselves. All these things that the prophet saw as future he narrated as past. Well, here it is also said like this: You blessed your land, O Lord, as if it had already been done. 4. You turned away the captivity of Jacob. Of his people, ancient Jacob, people of Israel, born of the lineage of Abraham, future heir of God by reciprocal promise. Those people were certainly where the Old Testament was given, but in the Old Testament the New was prefigured. That captivity was a symbolism; This is a manifestation of the truth. In that symbolism, according to a certain prediction of the future, the land of promise was given to that people, in a certain region where the Jewish people lived, in which the city of Jerusalem was located, whose name we have all heard of. When that people received this land, they endured many annoyances from their neighboring enemies, who hostilely surrounded them on all sides. But when Pepe went against his God, he was delivered into captivity, not for his perdition, but for his correction; not by condemning the father, but by correcting with punishment. When those people were corrected, they were forgiven; for sometimes he was taken captive and delivered. Now he is also in captivity due to the enormous sin of having crucified his Master. How, then, will we take, considering

bald? Non ut irrideamus illum, sed ut ploremus ante illum. Nam irriserunt quídam, et a daemonibus vastad sunt: ​​quomodo in Regnorum libro calvum Elisaeum irriserunt pueri, dicebantque post illum, Calve, calve; processerunt ursi de silva, et comedeiunt pueros male tidentes (4 Reg 2,23.24), et plangendos a parentibus suis. Significavit hoc factum prophetia quadam, futurum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Ule enim a Iudaeis irridentibus velut calvus itrisus est, quia in Calvariae loco crucifixus est (Mt 27:31). Nos autem si in illum crediderimus, filii ipsius sumus. Nobis etgo cantatur iste psalmus, ubi insctibitur, filiis Core: sumus enim filii sponsi (Mt 9:15). Ule quippe sponsus, dans arrham sponsae suae, sanguinem suum et Spiritum sanctum, quo locupletavit nos interim in this peregrinatione; adhuc autem servat nobis occultas divitias suas. Unde enim tale pignus dedit, quid est quod servat? 3 [v.2]. Itaque cantat ei Propheta in futurum, et utitur verbis quasi iam praeteriti temporis; tanquam facta dicit, quaefutura erant: quia apud Deum et quod futurum est, iam factum est. Ibi ergo Propheta videbat future nobis, iam vero facta in illius providentia et praedestinatione certissima, quomodo dicit et in lio psalmo ubi omnes Christum agnoscimt; sic enim recitatur, tanquam Evangelium legatur: "Foderunt manus meas et pedes, dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea; ipsi vero consideraverunt et conspexerunt me, diviserunt sibj ropa mea et super vestem meam

miserunt sortem" (Ps 21,17-19). Quis non, legente lectore Psalmum, agnoscat Evangelium? Et tamen cum diceretur in Psalmo, non dictum est, Fossuri sunt manus meas et pedes; sed, foderunt manus meas et pedes: nec dictum est, Dinumeraturi sunt ossa mea; sed, dinumeraverunt ossa mea: nec dictum est, Divisuri sunt ropa mea; sed, diviserunt sibi ropa mea. Haec omnia quaefutura videbat Propheta, tanquam praeterita indicabat: sic et hic, Benedixisti, Domine, terram tuam; tanquam iam fecerit. 4. Avertisti captivitatem lacob. Populus eius antiquus Iacob, populus Israel, natus de semine Abrahae, in repromissione futurus aliquando haeres Dei. Erat quidem ergo Ule populus, cui datum est Testamentum Vetus; sed in Vetere Testament figurabatur Testamentum Novum: illa figura erat, haec expressio veritatis. In illa autem figura secundum quamdam praenuntiationemfuturum, data est illi populo terra quaedam promissionis, in quadam regione ubihabitat populus Iudaeorum; ubi est etiam Ierusalem civitas, cuius nomen omnes audivimus. Hanc ergo terram cum accepisset ille populus, ab hostibus suis vicinis circumquaque inimicantibus fines inconveniences patiebatur: et cum peccabat in Deum suum, ibatur in captivitatem; non ad interitum, sed ad disciplinam; non damnante patre, sed flagellante. Et cum possessa esset, liberabatur, et aliquoties captivata est et liberata est illa gens: et moda in captivitate

the Jews, what is said: Did you turn away the captivity of Jacob? Or is this another captivity from which we all wish to be free? Because it is true that we all belong to Jacob if we belong to the lineage of Abraham. Given this, the Apostle says: From Isaac your offspring will be called, that is, the children of the flesh are not the children of God, but the children of the promise are those counted by descent. If the children of the promise are those counted by descent, the Jews offending God, they degenerated; and we, gaining unto God, not belonging to the flesh but to faith, became of the seed of Abraham. Imitating their faith we became their children; but they, departing from the faith, deserved to be disinherited. So that you may know that they have lost the genealogy of Abraham, observe that, when they boasted arrogantly, having heard our Lord Jesus Christ speak, and gloried in the blood and not in the life, and said to the Lord: We have Abraham as our father, the Lord answered them as degenerates: If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham. Therefore, if they were no longer children of Abraham because they did not perform his works, therefore we are children of Abraham since we do them. What are the works of Abraham that we perform? Abraham believed God and righteousness was imputed to him. Then we will all belong to Jacob imitating the faith of Abraham, who believed God and was imputed to righteousness. What, then, is that captivity from which we wish to free ourselves? I think that none of us is now under the domination of barbarians, and I believe that no nation has burst upon us armed and nost, et hoc pro peccato magno, quod Dominum suum crucifixit. Quid igitur secundum istos accipimus, quod ait, Avertisti captivitatem lacob? An forte intelligimus hic alliam captivitatem, de qua omnes nos volumus liberai? Nam omnes pertinemus ad lacob, si pertinemus ad semen Abrahae. Hoc enim dicit Apostolus: ln Isaac vocabitur tibí semen; id est, non hi qui filii carnis, hi filü Dei, sed filii promissionis deputantur in semen (Rom 9,7.8). Si filii promissionis in semen deputantur, offendendo Deum Iudaei degeneraverunt; nos promerendo Deum, de genere Abrahae facti sumus, non pertinent ad carnem, sed pertinent ad fidem.

Imitati enim fidem, filii facti sumus: illi autem degenerando a fide, exhaeredari meruerunt. Nam, ut noveritis quia perdiderunt illud, quod nati erant of Abraham, cum se arroganter iactarent audiente Domino Iesu Christo, gloriantes de sanguine et non de vita, et dicerent Domino, Nos patrem habemus Abraham; ait illis Dominus tanquam degenerantibus: Si filii Abrahae estis, facia Abrahae facite (lo 8,39). Si ergo illi propterea iam non filii, quia non faciebant facta Abrahae; nos propterea filii, quia fací mus íacta Abrahae. Quae sunt facta Abrahae quae facimus? Credidit autem Abraham Deo, et deputatum est illi ad iustitiam (Gen 15,6 et Gal 3,6). Ergo omnes ad lacob pertinemus, imitantes Abrahae fidem, qui credidit Deo, et deputatum est illi ad iustitiam. Quae est ergo illa captivitas unde nos volumus liberai? puto enim neminem nostrum moda esse apud Barbaros, nec aliquam gentem irruisse armatam, et captivos duxisse nos. Sed moda ostendo quamdam captivitatem, in qua gemi-

led to captivity. However, now I show you a certain captivity in which we find ourselves groaning and from which we wish to be free. The apostle Saint Paul comes out in the middle and explains it. Let him be our mirror, let him speak and we see ourselves reflected in him. There is no one who is not recognized here. The blessed Apostle says: I am pleased in the law of God according to the inner man; Inwardly I delight in the law of God; But I see another law in my members that fights against the law of? nor mind. You have heard the law, you have heard the struggle, you have not yet heard the captivity; hear the things that follow: That he fights, he says, against the law of my mind, and holds me captive in the law of sin that exists in my members. We knew captivity. Who is there among us who does not want to be freed from this captivity? And how will he be delivered, since what is to happen is sung in the same psalm, as in the past, in this way: You removed the captivity of Jacob? Who was addressed? To Christ, then write: For the end, for the sons of Korah. Christ, then, turns away the captivity of Jacob. He also hears Saint Paul himself who affirms it. After having said that he is captive by the law that exists in his members and that he fights against the law of his mind, he exclaims being under that captivity and says: Unhappy man I am. Who will free me from this body of death? He investigated who could deliver him, and instantly it occurred to him: The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. About this grace of God the prophet says to this Lord of ours Jesus Christ: You removed the captivity of Jacob. See the captivity of Jacob; See, that you removed our captivity consists, not in freeing us from the barbarians, into whose hands we have not fallen, but in freeing us from the works mus, et unde nos liberai cupimus. Paulus apostolus proceedat, ipse illam dicat; sit ipse speculum nostrum, ille loquatur, et nos ibi videamus: nemo est enim qui non hic se agnoscat. Ait ergo ille beatus apostolus, Condelector enim legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem; intus delectat me lex Dei: video autem aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentís meae. Iam audisti legem, audisti pugnam; captivitatem nondum audieras, audi quae sequuntur: Repugnantem, inquit, legi mentís meae, et captivum me ducentem in lege peccati, quae est in membris meis. Agnovimus captivitatem: quis nostrum est qui nolit se de ista captivitate liberai?

Et unde liberabitur? Quoniam hoc cantavit ipse Psalmus futurum: Avertisti captivitatem lacob. Cui dixit? Christo, propter ln finem, propter filios Core: ille enim avertit captivitatem lacob. Audi et ipsum Paulum confitentem. Cum diceret se trahi captivum a lege in membris suis repugnante legi mentís suae, exclamavit sub illa captivitate, et ait: lnfelix ego homo, quis liberabit me de corpore mortis huius? Quaesivit quis esset, et statim illi oceurrit, Gratia Dei per lesum Christum Dominum nostrum (Rom 7,22-25). De hac gratia Dei Propheta dicit huic Domino nostro Iesu Christo, Avertisti captivitatem lacob. Attendite captivitatem lacob, attendite quia hoc est, Avertisti captivitatem nostram: non liberando nos a Barbaris in quos non incurrimus; sed liberating us ab operibus malis, a peccatis nostris, per quae nobis satan dominabatur. If you want enim

bad, in freeing us from our sins, by which Satan subjugates us. If anyone has been freed from his sins, there will be no way for the prince of sinners to dominate him. 5 [v.3.4]. How did he turn away Jacob's captivity? See that this liberation is spiritual; See that he takes Cíibo inside. You sent iniquity to your people; You covered up all their sins. This is how he turned away captivity: forgiving iniquity. Iniquity held you captive; iniquity destroyed, you are now free. Confess that you are in captivity so that you deserve to be delivered. For he who does not know his enemy, how is he to call upon his deliverer? You covered up all my sins. What does you cover up mean? Make sure you don't see them. What does it mean to hide them? Don't punish them. You did not want to see our sins, and you did not see them because you did not want to. You covered up all our sins. You appeased all your anger; you desisted from the wrath of your indignation. 6 [v. 5]. And since all these things refer to the future tense, since the words are recorded in the past tense, he continues and says: Convert us, O God of our health! Why does he pray that what he now narrated as having already happened would happen if it were not because he wanted to show that he spoke in the past tense in the prophecy? What he said had happened has not yet happened, and he proves it because he prays it will take place. Convert us, O God of our healings!, and turn away your wrath from us. Not long ago you said: You turned away the captivity of Jacob; you covered up all their sins; you appeased all your anger; you desisted from the wrath of your indignation

tion. How do you say now turn your anger from us? The prophet answers you: I express as fulfilled what I see must be fulfilled; But since it has not been fulfilled, I pray that it may be fulfilled as I saw that it must be fulfilled. Turn away your anger from us. 7 [v. 6]. Don't be eternally angry with us. By the wrath of God we are mortal, and by the wrath of God we eat bread in this life in poverty and with the sweat of our face. This is what Adam heard when he sinned, and we were all that Adam because we all died in him. What he heard happened to us too. We did not yet exist, but we were in Adam. Therefore, whatever happened to him, happened to us; luckily we died in it, since we were all in it. The sins that born parents and children commit are not imputed to the children. The children born belong to each other, and the parents belong to themselves too. Therefore, those who were born, if they retained the perverse ways of their parents, it is necessary that they also endure their merits; But, if they change and do not imitate bad parents, they begin to have their own merit, but not that of their parents. Your father's sin does not harm you to such an extent if you had changed, that your father's sin would harm him if he had converted. But what our root already received in order to mortality, it dragged from Adam. What did he drag? The fragility of the flesh, the torment of pain, this house of poverty, this bond of death and the bonds of temptations. We carry all these things in the flesh, and they are the wrath of God because they are punishments from him. But as it happened

liberatus fuerit a peccatis suis, non habet unde illi dominetut princeps peccatorum. 5 [v.3.4]. Quomodo enim avertit captivitatem Iacob? Videte quia ista liberatio spiritualis est, videte quia intus agitur: Remisisti, inquit, iniquitatem plebis tuae; operuisti omnia peccata eorum. Ecce unde avertit captivitatem, quia remisit iniquitatem: iniquitas tenebat captivum, remissa iniquitate liberais. Confitere ergo te esse in captivitate, ut dignus sis liberari: nam qui hostem suum non intellexit, quomodo invoket liberatorem? Operuisti omnia peccata eorum. Quid est, operuisti? Ut non illa videres. Quid est, ut non illa videres? Ut non in ¡Ha vindicares. Noluisti videre peccata nostra; et ideo non vidisti, quia ipsa videre noluisti: Operuisti omnia peccata eorum. Sedasti omnem iram tuam; avertisti ab ira indignationis tuae. 6 [v.5]. Et quoniam defuture ista dicuntur, quamvis verba praeterita sonent; sequitur, et dicit: Converte nos, Domine sanitatum nostrarum. Quod moda narrabat quasi factum esset, quomodo orat ut fiat; nisi quia voluit ostendere praeterita verba se in prophetia dixisse? Nondum autem factum esse quod dicebat iam factum, hinc ostendit, quia orat ut fiat: "Converte nos, Domine sanitatum nostrarum; et averte iracundiam tuam a nobis." Non iamdudum dicebas, "Avcrtisti captivitatem fecob; operuisti omnia peccata eorum: sedasti omnem iram tuam; aversus es ab ira indignationis tuae?" Quomodo hic, "Et averte iracundiam mam a nobis?"

Respondet tibi Propheta: Illa dico quasi facta, quia future video; quia vero nondum facta sunt, oro ut veniant, quae iam vidi. Averte iracundiam tuam a nobis. 7 [v.6]. Non in aeternum irascaris nobis. De ira Dei enim mortales sumus, et de ira Dei in ista terra in egestate et labore vultus nostri manducamus panem. Hoc enim audivit Adam, quando peccavit (Gen 3 19); et Adam ille omnes nos eramus, quia in Adam omnes moriuntur: quod ille audivit, secutum est et nos. Non enim eramus iam nos, sed eramus in Adam: ideo quidquid evenit ipsi Adam, secutum est et nos, ut moreremur; omnes quippe in illo Fuimus. Ea enim peccata parentum non pertinent ad filios quae faciunt parentes iam natis filiis: iam enim nati filii ad se pertinent, et parentes ad se pertinent. Itaque illi qui nati sunt, si tenuerint vias parentum suorum malas, necesse est portent et merita ipsorum: si autem mutaverint se, et non fuerint imitati parentes malo, incipiunt habere meritum suum, non meritum parentum suorum. Usque adeo autem non tibi obest peccatum patris tui, si te mutaveris, ut nec ipsi patri tuo obsit, si se mutaverit. Be iam quod accepit ad mortalitatem istam radix nostra, duxit of Adam. Quid duxit? Istam fragilitatem carnis, hoc tormentum dolorum, hanc domum paupertatis, hoc vinculum mortis, et laqueos tentationum: portamus omnia ista in carne hac; et ira Dei est ist, quia vindicta Dei est. Sed quia futurum erat ut regeneraremur, et credendo riovj eíficeremur, atque in resurrectione

to hope that we would reign, and believing we would be renewed, and all this mortality would disappear with the resurrection, and the ancient nobility of the whole man would be restored; Just as all died in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. Seeing this the prophet exclaims: Do not be eternally angry with us nor spread your anger from generation to generation. The first generation was mortal because of your anger; the second will be immortal in attention to your mercy. 8 [v. 7]. But what? Did you provide for yourself, O man, the merit of God's mercy by having converted to him, in such a way that those who did not convert did not obtain mercy, but instead obtained anger? How could you have converted if you had not been called? Didn't the one who called you separated help you convert? Do not assume the same conversion to yourself, because if he had not called you who was fleeing, you would not have been able to convert. Therefore, the prophet attributing the benefit of this conversion to God, prays and says: O God, by converting you will give life to us. We do not convert to you as if we did it spontaneously for ourselves without your mercy, and then you quicken us; but by converting you will quicken us; so that not only our vivification is due to you, but also the conversion itself to be vivified. O God, converting you will quicken us; and your people will rejoice in you. For his evil he rejoices in himself, for his good he rejoices in you. When he wants to have joys emanating from himself, he finds crying itself. But now, since all our joy is God, he who wants to rejoice confidently rejoices in him who does not omnis illa mortalitas absumeretur, et novitas totius hominis repararetur; sicut enim in Adam omnes moriuntur, sic et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur (1 Cor 15,22): hoc videns Propheta ait, Non in aeternum irascaris nobis, vel extendas iram tuam a generatione in generationem. I was prima generatio mortalis de ira tua; erit alters generatio immortalis de misericordia tua. 8 [v.7]. Quid ergo? hoc tibi tu praestitisti, o homo, ut quia conversus es ad Deum, merereris misericordiam ipsius; qui autem conversi non sunt, non sunt adepti misericordiam, sed invenerunt iram? Quid autem, ut convertereris, posses, nisi vocareris? Nonne ille qui te vocavit aversum, ipse praestitit ut convertereris?

Noli tibi ergo arrogare nec ipsam conversionem; Quia nisi te ille vocaret fugientem, non posses convertí. Propterea et ipsius conversionis beneficium Deo tribuens Propheta, hoc orat, et dicit: Deus, tu convertens vivificabis nos. Et non quasi nos ipsi nostra sponte sine mercy tua convertimur ad te, et tu -vivificabis nos: sed, tu convertens vivificabis nos; ut non solum vivificatio nostra a te sit, sed etiam ipsa conversio ut vivificemur. Deus tu convertens vivificabis nos; et plebs tua laetabitur in te. Malo suo laetabitur in se; bonus suo laetabitur in te. Quando enim voluit habere gaudia de se, invenit planctum in se: nunc vero quia totum gaudium nostrum Deus est, qui vult securus gaudere, in lio gaudeat, qui non potest perire.

can perish. Why, my brothers, do you want to rejoice in silver? Either she perishes, or you; and no one knows who will perish first; It is only certain that both things must perish. Who must perish first? We ignore it. Neither man nor money can always remain in this world. We will say the same about the gold, the clothing, the house, the money, the extensive estate; in short, of this light. Do not rejoice in these things; rejoice in that indeficient light; Rejoice in that light which was not preceded by yesterday nor followed by tomorrow. What is this light? I am, says Christ, the light of the world. Whoever tells you: I am the light of the world, calls you to himself. When he calls you, he converts you; when he converts you, he heals you; When I have healed you, you will see your Converter, to whom it is said: And your people will rejoice in you. 9 [v. 8]. Show us, Lord, your mercy. We have sung this; and I already talked about it. Show us, Lord, your mercy, and give us your health. Your health, your Christ. Happy is he to whom God showed his mercy. He whom God showed his mercy cannot be arrogant; Because by showing him his mercy he makes him see that whatever good man himself has, he has it only through Him Who is our absolute Good; And when man sees that all the good he has does not come from himself, but comes from God, he realizes that everything he praises himself comes from the mercy of God, not from his own merits; and so, seeing these things, he does not become arrogant; and, not being arrogant, do not be conceited or exalted; and, not exalting himself, he does not fall; and, not falling, will Quid enim, fratres mei, gaudere vultis in argento? Aut argentum perit, aut tu; et nemo scit quid prius: verumtamen illud constat, quia utrumque periturum est; quid prius, incertum est. Nam nec homo hic potest manere semper, nec argentum hic potest manere semper; sic aurum, sic vestís, sic domus, sic pecunia, sic lata praedia, sic postremo lux ista. Noli ergo veüe gaudere in istis: sed gaude in illa luz quae non habet occasum; gaude in illa luz quam non praecedit hesternus dies, nec sequitur crastinus. What is this lux? Ego sum, inquit, lux mundi (lo 8,12). Qui tibi dicit, Ego sum lux mundi, vocat te ad se. Cum vocat te, convertit te; cum convertit te, sanat te; cum sanaverit te, videbis conversorem tuum, cui dicitur, Et plebs tua laetabitur in te. 9 [v.8].

Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam. Hoc est quod cantavimus, et iam hinc diximus. Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam; et salutare tuum da nobis: salutare tuum, Christum tuum. If he wants to straighten men's hearts to himself, he will fall with them. What seems better to you, that you fall with him for whom you are going, or that you remain standing with him for whom you convert? Our joy, our peace, our rest, the end of all work, is God alone. Blessed are those who direct their hearts to him. 11 [v. 10]. Certainly his health is close to those who fear him. Among the Jews there were some who already feared him. In all the roundness of the earth idols were worshiped; demons were feared, not God; However, in the Jewish nation God was feared. But why was he feared? They were feared in the Old Testament so that they would not be delivered into captivity, so as not to lose possession of the promised land, so that their vineyards would be stoned, their wives would be barren, they would lose their children. These promises of God restrained faint-hearted souls, and because of them God was feared; However, he was with those who feared him because of these things. The pagan asked the devil for the land; the Jew asked God for it; The request was identical, but it was not the same person who was asked for it. The Jew asking for the same thing as the pagan, nevertheless he was distinguished from the pagan, because he asked it of him who created all things; and, therefore, the God who was far from the nations was with them. However, he looked with compassion on those who were far away and on those who were near, as the Apostle says: And when he came, he evangelized peace to you who were far away, and peace to those who were near. Who did he say were close to? Of the Jews, because they worshiped only God. Quid est melius, ut cadas cum illo ad quem converteris, ao ut stes cum illo cum quo converteris? Who did he say were far away from? Of the Gentiles, because they had turned away from him for whom they were made and worshiped the things they had made. No one is distant from God by space, but by the heart. Do you love God? You are close. Do you hate him? You are far away. Being in the same place, you are close and far away. Then, brothers, the prophet contemplated these things; and although he saw the universal mercy of God upon all nations, yet he observed something special and peculiar in the Jewish nation, and that is why he says: Indeed, I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people. But his people will not be the Jewish nation alone, but will be gathered together from all nations, for he will speak peace to his saints and to all those who turn their hearts to him; and all those who will direct their hearts to God will come from all nations. Certainly his health is close to those who fear him; so that glory may dwell in our land, that is, so that the land in which the prophet was born may have the greatest glory, because from there Christ began to be announced. From there and there the apostles were first sent. The prophets were from there; The temple was first built there; there it was sacrificed to God; from there were the patriarchs, there came He Himself, coming from the lineage of Abraham; there Christ was manifested and there he appeared; because from there was the Virgin Mary who gave birth to Christ. There he walked on foot, there he worked wonders. Finally, he gave so much honor to that people that, when a certain Canaanite woman intercepted him on his way seeking health for her daughter, he replied: I was only sent to the sheep that perished from the house of Israel. Ergo, Misericordia et veritas occurrerunt sibi; iustitia et pax osculatae sunt se.

Fac iustitiam, et habebis pacem; ut osculentur se iustitia et pax. Si enim non amaveris iustitiam, pacem non habebis: amant enim se duo ista, iustitia et pax, et osculantur se; ut qui fecerit iustitiam, inveniat pacem osculantem iustitiam. Duae amicae sunt; tu forte unam vis, et altetam non facis: nemo est enim qui non vult pacem; sed non omnes volunt operani iustitiam. Interroga omnes homines: Vis pacem? One prays tibi responds totum genus humanum: Opto, cupio, voló, amo. Ama et iustitiam; quia duae amicae sunt iustitia et pax; ipsae se osculantur: si amicam pacis non amaveris, non te amabit ipsa pax, nec veniet ad te. Quid enim magnum est desiderare pacem? Qui vis malus desiderat pacem. Bona enim res est pax. Be fac iustitiam; quia iustitia et pax se osculantur, non litigant. Do you quare litigates cum iustitia? Ecce iustitia dicit

Once this is done, you will not look for her for long, because she herself will come out to meet you to kiss justice. 13 [v. 12]. Truth was born from the earth, and justice looked down from heaven. The truth was born from the earth. Christ was born of woman. The truth was born from the earth. The Son of God came from the flesh. What is the truth? The Son of God. What is the earth? The meat. Investigate where Christ was born, and you will see that truth was born from the earth. But this truth that was born from the earth existed before the earth, and by it the heaven and the earth were made. But so that justice might look down from heaven, that is, so that men might be justified by divine grace, truth was born from the Virgin Mary so that she could offer the sacrifice on behalf of those who were to be justified: the sacrifice of the passion, the sacrifice of the cross. How could he have offered the sacrifice for our sins if he had not died? And how could he have died if he had not received from us what to die for? That is, if Christ had not taken mortal flesh from us, he would not have been able to die, because he does not die tibi, Ne furetis; et non audis: Ne adulteres; non vis audire: Non facías alteri quod tu pati non vis, non dicas alteri quod et tibi dici non vis. Inimicus is amicae meae, dicit tibi pax; why do you like me? Amica sum iustitiae, quemcumque inveneto inimicum amicae meae, non ad illum accesso. Vis ergo come ad pacem? Fac iustitiam. Ideo alius psalmus dicit tibi: Decline to malo, et fac bonum (hoc est amate iustitiam); et cum iam declinaveris to malo, et fecetis bonum, quaere pacem, et persequere eam (Psalm 33:15). Iam enim non diu illam quaeres, quia et ipsa occurret tibi, ut osculetur iustitiam. 13 [v.12].

Veritas de terra orta est, et iustitia de cáelo prospexit. Veritas de terra orta est: Christus de femina natus est. Veritas de terra orta est: Filius Dei de carne processit. Who is veritas? Filius Dei. Quid est titta? Cato. Interroga unde natus est Christus, et vides quia veritas de terra orta est. Sed haec veritas quae orta est de terra, erat ante terram, et per ipsam factum est caelum et tetta; sed ut iustitia de cáelo ptospiceret, id est, ut iustificatentur homines divina gratia, veritas nata est de Maria virgine; ut posset pto illis iustificandis offerre sacrificium, sacrificium passionis, sacrificium crucis. Et unde offerret sacrificium pro peccatis nostris, nisi moreretur? unde autem moreretur, nisi a nobis acciperet ubi moreretur? Id est, nisi a nobis sumeret carnem mortalem, Christus

the Word; divinity does not die; The power and wisdom of God does not die. And how would he have offered the sacrifice, the victim of health, if he had not died? You were a sinful man. You, oh earth, who when you sinned heard: you are earth and to earth you will go; May truth be born from you so that justice may look from heaven. How does the truth come from you being a sinner, being perverse? Confess your sins and the truth will be born from you. If, being wicked, you confess that you are wicked, the truth was born from the earth. Behold the publican praying in the temple far from the Pharisee, who did not even dare to lift his eyes to heaven, but smote his chest, saying: Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner. This is how the truth of the earth was born when confession was carried out by man. What's next? Truly I tell you that the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The truth was born from the earth in the confession of sins; and justice looked down from heaven so that the publican would come down justified rather than the Pharisee. So that you may know that the truth belongs to the confession of sins, Saint John the Evangelist says: If we said that we do not have morí non posset; Quia Verbum non moritur, divinitas non monta, Virtus et Sapientia Dei non moritur. How do I offerret sacrificium victimam salutarem, si non moreretur? quomodo autem moreretur, nisi carnem indueret? quomodo carnem indueret, nisi veritas de terra oriretur? Sales of terra orta est, et iustitia de cáelo prospexit. 14. Possumus hinc dicere alterum sensum. Veritas de terra orta est: confessio ab nomine. Homo enim peccator eras. O terra, qui quando peccasti, audisti, Terra es, et in terram ibis (Gen 3:19), oriatur de te veritas, ut respiciat de cáelo iustitia. How to te oritur veritas, cum tu peccator sis, cum tu iniquus sis? Confitete peccata tua, et orietur de te veritas. Si enim cum sis iniquus, dicis te iustum, how do you veritas oriretur?

Si autem cum sis iniquus, you say te iniquum; veritas de terra orta est. Intend illum Publicanum longe a Pharisaeo in Templo Orantem, qui ñeque oculos ad caelum audebat levare, sed percutiebat pectus suum, dices, Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori: ecce veritas de terra orta est, quia confessio peccatorum ab homine facta est. Quid ergo sequitur? Amen dico vobis, quia descendit iustificatus Pubücanus Ule magis quam Ule Pharisaeus: quia omnis qui se exalut, htimiliabitur; et qui se humiliat, exaltabitur (Luke 18,13,14). Orta est veritas de terra, in confessione peccatorum; et iustitia de cáelo prospexit, ut descenderet iustificatus Pubücanus ille magis quam ille Pharisaeus. Nam ut noveritis quia veritas pertinet ad confessionem peccatorum, ait Ioannes evangelista: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et veritas in nobis

sins, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. How is truth born from the earth so that justice can be seen from heaven? Then truth was born from the earth, and justice looked down from heaven. How did justice look from heaven? God saying: Let us forgive this man who did not forgive himself, we excuse him because he did not excuse himself. His sin was punished, I will deliver him. We have one verse left; I ask that fatigue does not appear in what I have to say. Pay attention, my brothers, to a very necessary thing. Pay attention, perceive, take with you and do not let the seed of God in your hearts be vain. The truth, he says, was born from the earth, that is, the confession of sins by man; and justice looked down from heaven, that is, justification was given by the Lord God to him who confessed, so that the wicked would recognize that he could not have become godly if He who confessed had not done so, believing in him who justifies the wicked. You can have sins; but you will not have good fruit if He Whom you confess does not give it to you. Therefore, after having said: Truth was born from the earth, and justice looked down from heaven, as if asked, what did you say when you said: Justice looked down from heaven?, he adds that the Lord will give softness, and the earth will give its fruit. Let's look at our interior, and if we only find p e non est. Quomodo ergo veritas de terra oritur, ut iustitia de cáelo prospiciat, audi illum sequentem et dicentem: Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est et iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata, et purget nos ab omni iniquitate (1 lo 1,8.9). Veritas ergo de terra orta est, et iustitia de cáelo prospexit. Quae iustitia de cáelo prospexit? Tanquam Dei dicetis: Parcamus huic homini, quia ipse sibi non pepercit; ignoscamus, quia ipse agnoscit. Conversus est ad puniendum peccatum suum; convert et ego ad eum liberandum. Veritas de terra orta est, et iustitia de cáelo prospexit. 15 [v.13]- Etenim Dominus dabit suavitatem, et terra nostra dabit fructum suum.

Unus versus restat, peto sine taedio sit quod dicturus sum. Attendite rem necessariam, fratres mei; attendite, percipite, auferte vobiscum, et non sit inane semen Dei in cordibus vestris. Veritas, inquit, de terra orta est, confessio peccatorum ab homine; et iustitia de cáelo prospexit, id est, a Domino Deo data est iustificatio confitenti, ut ipse agnoscat impius pium se fieri non posse, nisi ille fecerit cui confitetur, credendo in eum qui iustificat impium (Rom 4,5). Tua ergo peccata potes habere; fructum bonum non habebis, nisi ille dederit cui confiteris. Ideo cum dixisset, Veritas de terra orta est, et iustitia de cáelo prospexit; tanquam diceretur ei, Quid est quod dixisti, Iustitia de cáelo prospexit? Etenim, inquit, Dominus dabit suavitatem et terra nostra dabit fructum suum. Nos ergo respiciamus nos; et si nihil in nobis invenerimus nisi peccata, oderimus peccata, et desideremus iustitiam. Cum enim coeperi

fallen, let us hate sins and desire justice. When we have begun to hate sins, the very hatred of sins begins to make us similar to God, because we hate what God hates. When we have begun to hate sins and confess God, by dragging you away to illicit delights and leading you to things that do not profit you, groan to God, and, confessing your sins, you will deserve His delight and He will give you the gentleness of operative justice so that justice begins to delight you, who first delighted in iniquity, so that you, who first rejoiced in iniquity, drunkenness, you rejoice in sobriety; and so that you, who at first rejoiced in the theft, taking from man what you did not have, may seek to give what you have to the one who lacks it; and in this way, whoever liked to steal, liked to give; He who loved to attend shows, loved to pray; He who delighted in frivolous and lascivious songs, took delight in singing hymns to God; and those who first ran to the theater now like to run to church. Where did this sweetness come from but that the Lord will give sweetness, and the earth will give its fruit? See what I say: I explained the word of God to you, I sowed the seed in the devout hearts, having found your chests furrowed with the plow of confession; With attention and devotion you received the seed, think about the word you heard lest the birds of the sky eat the seed. Be like a plowed and threshed land so that what was sown can germinate there. But, if God does not rain, what is the point of having sown? That is: the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit. He, then, with his visits at rest, at work, at home, in bed, in banmus odisse peccata, iam ipsum odium peccatorum similes nos incipit faceré Deo; quia hoc odimus quod odit et Deus.

Cum ergo coeperis odisse peccata et confiten Deo, cum te delectationes illicitae rapiunt et ducunt ad ea quae tibi non prosunt, ingemisce ad Deum: et confitens illi peccata tua, mereberis ab illo delectationem, et suavitatem iustitiae faciendae dabit tibi, ut incipiat te delectare iustitia, quem primo delectabat iniquitas; ut qui primo gaudebas in ebrietate, gaudeas in sobrietate; et qui primo gaudebas de furris, ut tolleres homini quod non habebas, quaeras donare non habenti quod habebas; et quem delectabat rappere, delectet donare; quem delectabat spectare, delectet orare; quem delectabant cantica nugatoria et adulterina, delectet hymnum dicere Deo; Currere ad ecclesiam, qui primo currebas ad theatrum. Unde nata est ista suavitas, nisi quia Dominus dabit suavitatem, et terra nos tu dabit fructum suutn? Ecce enim videte quod dico: ecce locuti sumos vobis verbum Dei, semen sparsimus devotis cordibus, tanquam sulcata invenientes pectora vestra aratro confessionis; devotione et intentione suscepistis semen, cogitate de verb quod audistis, tanquam glebas frangentes, ne semen rapiant volatilia, ut possit ibi germinare quod seminatum est; et nisi Deus pluerit, quid prodest quod seminatur? Hoc est, Dominas dabit suavitatem, et terra riostra dabit fructum suum. lile enim visitationibus suis, in otio, in

May I, in the conversation, in the walk, visit your hearts where I am not. God's rain will come and what was sown there will bear fruit. And where I am not, either because I rest confidently, or because I dedicate myself to something else, may God give an increase to the seeds that I have sown so that, later contemplating your good habits, I may rejoice in the fruit. For the Lord will give softness, and our land will give its fruit. 16 [v.14]. Justice will go before him, and will set his steps in the way. Justice is that which occurs in the confession of sins. The truth is itself. You must be fair to yourself by punishing yourself. For the first justice of man consists in punishing yourself by being bad, so that in this way God can make you good. Since this is the first justification of man, it becomes a way for God so that God may draw near to you. Make the way for him with the confession of sins. Hence Saint John, when baptizing with water as a sign of penitence and wanting those who repented of their first acts to come to him, said: Prepare the way to the Lord; make your paths straight. You took pleasure, oh man, in your sins; Dislike what you were so that you can be what you were not. Prepare the way to the Lord. Let this justice precede you, that you confess your sins; and so he will come and visit you, because he will place his steps on the path, because he already has a place to establish his steps, he already has a place to come to you. Before you confessed your sins you had blocked God's way to reach you; I had no path to approach you. Confess your life, and you will open the way; and Christ will come to you, and will place his steps on the path to instruct you and guide you with his footprints. negotio, in domo, in lecto, in convivio, in collocutione, in ambulatione vísitet corda vestra, ubi nos non sumus. Veniat imber Dei, et fructificet quod ibi seminatum est; et ubi non sumus nos, et securi quiescimus, aut aliud agimus, Deus det incrementum seminibus quae sparsimus, ut attendentes postea bonds mores vestros, etiam de fructu gaudeamus: Quoniam Dominus dabit suavitatem, et terra nostra dabit fructum suum. 16 [v.14]. Iustitia ante eum praeibit, et ponet in via gressus suos. Iustitia illa est quae est in confessione peccatorum: veritas enim ipsa est. lustus enim deben esse in te, ut punías te: ipsa est prima hominis iustitia, ut punías te malum, et faciat te Deus bonum.

Quia ergo ipsa est prima hominis iustitia, ipsa fit via Deo, ut veniat ad te Deus: ibi illi fac viam, in confessione peccatorum. Ideo et Ioannes cum baptizaret in aqua poenitentiae, et vellet ad se vinore poenitentes de suis prioribus factis, hoc dicebat: Párate viam Domino, rectas facite semitas eius (Mt 3,3). Placebas tibi in peccatis tuis, or homo; displiceat tibi quod eras, ut possis esse quod non eras. Párate viam Domino: praecedat ista iustitia, ut confitearis peccata: veniet ille et visitabit te, quia ponet in via gressus suos; est enim iam ubi ponat gressus suos, est ubi ad te veniat. Ante autem quam confitereris peccata, intercluseras ad te viam Dei; non erat qua ad te vinoet. Confitere vitam, et aperis viam; et veniet Christus, et ponet in via gressus suos, ut te informat vestigiis suis.

God cannot give any greater gift to men than to make his Word, by whom he created all things, their Head and to adapt them to him as members, so that he would be the Son of God and the son of man; one God with the Father and one man with men. Therefore, when we speak to God in supplication, we do not separate the Son from the prayer; and when the Body of the Son prays, it does not remove its Head from itself; and so is the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Savior of his Body, who also asks for us and in us; and we also pray. Pray for us as our priest; pray in us as our Head; and we pray to Him as our God. Let us recognize our voice in Him, and His voice in us. Let us not hesitate when something is said, and especially prophetically, about our Lord Jesus Christ that indicates a certain baseness unworthy of God, attributing it to Him, who did not hesitate to join us. Since all creation serves Him, since it was created by Him. Hence, when we perceive his divinity and majesty by hearing in the beginning it was the Word, and the Word was next to God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. tempering this sublime divinity of the Son of God, who surpasses all the most excellent creatures; and, on the other hand, we also hear somewhere in Scripture that he groans, prays and confesses, we doubt attributing these words to him, due to the thought we have had about his recent contemplation of divinity, and the thought feels repugnance descending into his humility, as if it would insult him if he recognized in the man the words that he addressed to God when he prayed; and that is why many times she gets pregnant and tries to change her mind; being thus that the Scripture only offers him the way of turning to Him and does not allow him to separate himself from Him. Then he stretches, and awakens in his faith, and sees that the One whom he had contemplated shortly before in the form of God, took the form of a servant and was made in the likeness of men and found in habit as a man, and he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, and that he also wanted to make the words of the psalm his own when he found himself hanging on the cross and saying: My God, my God, why did you abandon me? Then He is asked in the form of God, and He prays in the form of a servant: there as Creator, here as created, taking without being changed the creature that is to be changed, and becoming one man, Head and Body. Then we pray to Him, through Him and in Him; and we speak with Him, and He speaks with us; and we recite in Him, and He recites in us the prayer of this psalm which is called the prayer of David, because our Lord, according to the flesh, is the son of David, although according to divinity he is Lord and Creator of David; which exists not only before David, but also before Abraham, whence David comes; and before Adam, et surplusem omnia creaturarum sublimia divinitatem Filii Dei, audimus etiam in aliqua parte Scripturarum velut gementem, orantem, confitentem; et dubitamus ei tribuere verba haec, ex eo quod cogitatio nostra de recenti eius contemplatione quae erat in divinitate, pigrescít descendé ad eius humilitatem; et tanquam faciat illi iniuriam, si eius verba in homine agnoscat, ad quem verba directionbat cum Deum deprecaretur, haeret plerumque, et conatur mutare sententiam; et non ei occurrit in Scriptura, nisi quod ad ipsum recurrat, et ab illo deviare non sinat.

Expergiscatur ergo, et evigilet in fide sua; et videat quia ille quem contemplabatur paulo ante in forma Dei, formam servi accepit, in similarityine hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut homo, humiliavit se factus obediens usque ad mortem (Phil 2,5-8); et verba Psalmi voluit esse sua, in cruz pendens, et dices: Deus meus, Deus meus, utquid me dereliquisti? (Ps 21,2). Oratur ergo in forma Dei, orat in forma servi: ibi Creator, hic creatus, creaturam mutandam non mutatus assumens, et secum nos faciens unum hominem, caput et corpus. Oramus ergo ad illum, per illum, in illo: et dicimus cum illo, et dicit nobiscum; dicimus in illo, dicit in nobis psalmi huius orationem, qui intitulatur, Oratio David. Quia Dominus noster secundum carnem filius David: secundum vero divinitatem Dominus David, et creator David; et non solum ante David, sed et ante Abraham, ex quo David; sed et ante Adam, ex quo omnes homines; thirst et ante caelum et terram, in quo omnis creature

No one, then, upon hearing these p; you speak, say: Christ does not speak, or likewise say, I do not speak; Rather, if you recognize that you are in the Body of Christ, say both things: Christ speaks and I speak. Don't speak anything without Him, because He doesn't speak anything without you. Is this not confirmed by the Gospel? There it was written: In the beginning was the Word and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made by Him; and there it is also recorded that Jesus was grieved, tired, slept, hungry, thirsty, prayed and spent entire nights in prayer; And he spent, says Saint Luke, the entire night praying, and also: and he remained in prayer and drops of blood ran down his body. What did he manifest when these drops of blood ran through his body? That his body, which is the Church, already distilled the blood of the martyrs. 2 [v.l}. Incline, Lord, your ear and listen to me. He says this regarding the form of a servant; You, O servant, as your Lord, say: Incline your ear, Lord. He inclines his ear if you are not conceited; He draws near to the humbled and turns away from the exalted if He had not exalted the one who humbled himself. God inclines his ear toward us. He is above, we are below; He is on high, we are low, but not abandoned, because God showed his love for us, because, even though we were sinners, Christ died for us. Hardly, says Saint Paul, is there anyone who dies for the righteous, although perhaps some dare to die for the good. Yet our Lord died for the wicked. Well, they did not precede

our merits for which the Son of God died, but rather because the merits were null, the mercy was great. With what sure and firm promise does He who gave his death to the wicked reserve eternal life for the righteous! Incline your ear, Lord, and listen to me, for I am poor and helpless. Therefore he does not incline his ear to the rich, but to the poor and helpless, to the humble and to the confessor; to the one who needs mercy. He does not incline his ear to the fed up and the conceited, to the one who boasts as if he lacked nothing and says: I thank you because I am not like this publican. The rich Pharisee boasted of his own merits; The poor publican confessed his sins. 3. But do not take, brothers, what I said, that God does not incline his ear towards the rich, as if he did not listen to those who have gold, silver, family and property. If perhaps you were born rich, or possess this state of worldly wealth, remember what the Apostle told you writing to Timothy: Command the rich of this world not to be arrogant. Those who do not become arrogant are poor in God; and to the poor, the destitute and the needy, he inclines his ear; for all of these understood that their hope should not be based either on gold, or on silver, or on the things in which they seem to temporarily abound. They are satisfied that the riches do not lose them; It is enough for them that they do not harm them, since they cannot benefit them in any way. What do I say? They can certainly serve as works of mercy to the rich and the poor: to the rich by desire and by work, and to the poor by desire alone.

When he is such that he despises in himself everything that pride uses to inflate itself, he is poor of God; and then God inclines his ear to him, for he sees his contrite heart. Without a doubt, brothers, we read and believe that the poor ulcer patient, who was lying before the rich man's door, was transported by the angels to Abraham's bosom. But the rich man, who dressed in purple and linen and ate richly every day, was taken to hell, to the place of torment. Was the poor man transported by angels rewarding his poverty, and, on the contrary, the rich man was sent to torment for the sin of his riches? In the poor, humility is glorified, and in the rich, pride is condemned. Briefly I prove that the rich man was not tormented by wealth, but by pride. Without a doubt the poor man was taken to Abraham's bosom; But of Abraham himself the Scripture says that he possessed abundant gold and silver in this world and that he was rich in the land. If the rich man is taken to torment, how had Abraham preceded the poor man in order to receive the one transported to his bosom? Because Abraham, in the midst of riches, was poor, humble, obedient to all the commandments. His riches were so worthless that God ordered him to immolate his son for whom he kept them. Both those who have something in this world and those who have nothing have learned to be neosy poor. For you also find the beggar who becomes arrogant and the wealthy who humbles himself. God opposes the proud, whether they are dressed in silk or rags; but gives grace to the humble, whether they have some worldly possessions, whether they lack

of them. God is an inspector of the interior; There he weighs, there he examines. You do not see the scales of God; your thoughts do not care about it. You see that he put the merit of hearing, that is, the reason for being heard in what he said: Because I am poor and helpless. See, maybe you're not poor or helpless. If you are not poor, you will not be heard. Everything that is around you or in you that you can boast about, throw it away from you. May God be all your presumption. Be destitute of Him so that you may be filled with Him. Everything you have without Him will serve as an immense void. 4 £v.2]. Guard my soul, for I am holy. I do not know that anyone could have said with complete truth: because I am holy, apart from Him who is without sin in this world and who is the forgiver of all sins, not the perpetrator of them. We recognize the voice of the one who says: because I am holy, keep my soul in that form of servant that I had taken. In her there is flesh and there is soul, since in that person there was not only flesh and Word, as some said, but flesh, soul and Word; and this all was one Son of God, one Christ, one Savior: in the form of God equal to the Father; and in the form of a servant, Head of the Church. Then when I hear: Because I am holy, I recognize his voice, and do I turn my voice away from it? When he speaks like this, he certainly speaks united to his Body. So, shall I dare to say: because I am holy? Christ, may that one man dare, who cries from the ends of the earth with his Head and under his Head, to say - because I am holy. For he received the gift of holiness, the grace of baptism, and the gift of the remission of sins. This you were, says the Apostle, enumerating many sins grave and light, ordinary and horrible; this you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified. If he says that we were sanctified, let each of the faithful also say: I am holy. This is not the arrogance of the conceited, but the confession of the grateful. If you say that you were holy because of yourself, you will be arrogant. Likewise, if, being faithful to Christ and a member of Christ, you say that you are not holy, you will be ungrateful. Censoring pride, the Apostle does not say that you lack everything, but rather, what do you have that you have not received? You are not censored for saying that you have what you have, but because you want what you have to come from you. Therefore, recognize that you possess and that nothing is your own, so that you will not be arrogant or ungrateful. Say to your God: I am holy because you sanctified me; because I received, not because I had; because you gave it to me, not because I deserved it. Otherwise you begin to insult our Lord Jesus Christ himself; Well, if all Christians, the faithful and those baptized into him, put on him, as the Apostle says: As many of you as were baptized into Christ put on Christ; If they became members of his Body and yet say that they are not holy, they insult the Head by not being holy members of it. See where you are, and accept the dignity of your Head. Indeed you were darkness, but now light in the Lord. In another time, says the same Apostle, you were Corpus Christi, audeat et unus ille homo clamans a finibus terrae (Ps 60,3), cum capite suo, et sub capite suo dicere, Quoniam sanctus sum. Accept enim gratiam sanctitatis, gratiam Baptismi et remissionis peccatorum. Et haec quidem fuestis, ait Apostolus, enumerans fines peecata, et levia et gravia, et usitata et horribilia: Et haec quidem ¡uistis; sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis (1 Cor 6:11). Si ergo sanctificatos dicit, dicat et unusquisque fidelium, Sanctus sum. Non est ista superbia elati, sed confessio non ingrati.

Si enim dixeris te ex te esse sanctum, superbus es: rursus, fidelis in Christo, et membrum Christi, si te dixeris non esse sanctum, ingratus es. Arguens enim superbiam Apostolus, non ait, Non habes; sed ait, Quid enim habes quod non aocepisti? (ibid. 4,7). Non arguebaris, quia dicebas te habere quod non habes; sed quia ex te tibi volebas esse quod habes. Imo et habere te agnosce, et ex te nihil habere, ut nec superbus sis, nec ingratus. Dec Deo tuo: Sanctus sum, quia sanctificasti me; quia accepi, non quia habui; quia tu dedisti, non quia ego merui. Etenim ex alio latere incipis iniuriam faceré ipsi Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Iam vide ubi sis, et de capite tuo dignitatem cape. Etenim eras in tenebris, nunc antem lux in Domino. Fuistis, inquit, aliquando tenebrae (Eph 5,8); sed numquid tenebrae remansistis? ad hoc

Since the Body of Christ groans in anguish until the end of the world, in which these tortures will cease to exist, man groans and cries out to God; and each of us cries out proportionately throughout this Body. You cried in your days, which are past; Another succeeds you and also cries out in his own days; you in yours, this one in his, and that one in his. The Body of Christ cries out at all times, both in the members that are passing and in those that are happening. A single man extends to the end of the world; for the identical members of Christ cry out: some already rest in Him; others cry out now, and others will cry out when we are dead; and after them others will continue crying. Here the psalmist listens to the voice of the entire Body of Christ that says: I cried to you all day long. same, how much less should we expect it to come from another? Or they are bad, and it is necessary to tolerate them and wait, because they can change; or they are good, and then it is better to love them, fearing that perhaps later they will be bad, because they can also change. In the former, their evil constitutes the bitterness of the soul; in the latter, the concern and fear that those who live well will fall. Wherever you turn you will find bitterness in earthly things; It has no way to be sweetened if it does not rise to God: because you, O Lord, are gentle and affable. What does it mean you are affable? May you carry me until you perfect me. Truly, my brothers, I will speak as a man among men and coming from men: let each one observe his heart and examine himself without flattery or flattery. There is nothing more foolish than flattering and deceiving oneself. Pay attention and see how many things the human heart thinks. Observe how vain thoughts often prevent prayer, in such a way that they barely allow the heart to be lifted up to God; and see how, striving to hold him close to God, he escapes in a certain way from himself and finds no barrier in which to enclose himself or any obstacle with which he can contain his distractions and wandering thoughts, and thus remain ready to be joyed by God. With difficulty it will happen that such a prayer does not occur among many. Some will say that it happens to him; another, that it does not happen to him. Well, we find in the divine books David praying in a certain circumstance and saying: Because I found, O Lord, my heart to pray with you. He says he found his heart as if he were used to running away from it; and, therefore, he pursues him like a fugitive and, since he cannot catch up with him, that is why he cries out to God: since my heart mutari possunt; aut boni sunt, et sic eos opportct diligere, ut timeamus (quia possunt mutari) ne mali sint: ibi malitia eorum facit amaritudinem animae; hic sollicitudo et timor, ne labatur qui bene ambulat. Quocumque ergo se converterit, in terrenis rebus amaritudinem invenit; unde dulcecat non habet, nisi levet se ad Deum. Quoniam tu, Domine, suavis et mitis. Who is mitis? abandoned me Therefore, my brothers, considering what is said here: You are gentle and gentle, it seems to me to be seeing what the word gentle contains here. Rejoice the soul of your servant, because you are gentle and gentle: I seem to see that it was said that God is gentle because he endures our things and, nevertheless, expects prayer from us to perfect us; and, when we address it to him, he receives it with pleasure and listens, and he does not remember how many we carelessly and without fervor we address to him, and he receives this only one that we hardly find good. What man is there, my brothers, who can tolerate a friend who has begun to talk to him, and, when he tries to respond to his conversation, sees him turn away from him and talk about something else to another? When will the judge tolerate you if perhaps you interrupted him and forced him to sit in court so that he could hear you and suddenly, while speaking to him, you abandon him and start chatting with a friend of yours? However, God tolerates so many hearts that pray and think so many different things; I fail to list the offensive ones, I fail to narrate those that are sometimes perverse and contrary to God. Thinking about the superfluous is already an insult done to the One with whom you had begun to talk. Your prayer is a locution with God. When you read, God speaks to you; When you pray, you speak to God. But what, should we despair of the human race and should we say that every man to whom, while praying, some thought had sneaked in and interrupted his prayer, should be condemned? If we said this, brothers, I don't see what hope there would be. Finally, as we have hope placed in God, since his mercy is great, let us say: Alegra Quoniam cor meum dereliquit me (Ps 39,13). Itaque, fratres mei, attendens quod hic ait, Suavis es tu et mitis; videor mihi videre hic quod ait, mitis. lucunda animam servi tui, quoniam ad te levavi animammeam; quoniam tu suavis et mitis es: videor mihi videre ad hoc dixisse mitem Deum, quia patitur ista nostra, et exspectat tamen a nobis orationem, ut perficiat nos; et quando illi eam dederimus, accipit grate, et exaudir, nec meminit tanta quas incondite fundimus, et accipit unam quam vix invenimus.

Quis enim est, fratres mei, homo, cum quo si coeperit amicus eius colloqui, et voluerit ille respondé collocutioni cius, et viderit eum averti a se, et aliud loqui ad alium, qui hoc ferat? Et toleratet Deus tot corda precantium, et diverse res cogitantium: omitto dicere et noxias, omitto dicere aliquando perversas et inimicas Deo; ipsas superfluas cogitare iniuria est eius, cum quo loqui coeperas. Until You do this, You tolerate me because You are gentle, O Lord, and gentle. 8. And exceedingly merciful. You are not only merciful, but extremely merciful. Our iniquity abounds, but your mercy is also multiplied. You are exceedingly merciful to all who call upon you. How do we understand what the Scripture says in many places: They will call on me and I will not hear them, while it is also true that he is merciful to all who call on him, but that some who call do not call on him?
