among those who call upon his name. They called on the Lord, and He heard them. From the pillar of cloud he spoke to them. These ancient servants of God, Moses, Aaron and Samuel, were great before the ancestors. You know that Moses, with the power of God, led the people of Israel out of Egypt through the Red Sea and guided them in the desert. The wonders that God worked at that time by the hand of Moses are known to all those who gladly hear the Scripture in the church, or! They read it privately, or learn it in some other way. Aaron was the brother of Moses, whom he ordained a priest. There it only seems that Aaron was a priest, since he is clearly called a priest of God in Scripture (in the Exodus). It is not expressly said there that Moses was a priest. But if it wasn't, what was it? Could he be more than a priest? This psalm expresses that it was, because it says: Moses and Aaron among his priests. Therefore they were priests of the Lord. Samuel's name appears later in the Book of Kingdoms. He lived in the time of David, for he anointed holy David. Samuel grew up in the temple from the early years of his childhood. His mother was barren; Wanting therefore to have a son, she prayed to the Lord with a loud groaning; By asking God to grant her a son to give to Him, she showed that she did not want to have, carried away by the flesh, the one who, when born, she gave up wanting him to be His. For she offered herself to the Lord, saying: If you would give me a male child, he will serve your temple, and so he did. When the holy Samuel was born, he was with his mother during breastfeeding; As soon as he removed him from his breast, he handed him over to the Lord so that there he might grow, there he would be strengthened in spirit, there he would serve God, being in qui invokent nomen eius. Invocabant Dominum., et ipse exaudiebat eos; in column nubis locobatur ad eos. Isti antiqui Moyses et Aaron et Samuel, serví Dei, magni apud antiquos. Nostis quia Moyses eduxit in virtute Dei populum Israel ex Aegypto per Rubrum mare; et duxit in eremo; et quanta mirabilia fecerit illo tempore Deus per manum Moysi, noverunt omnes qui istas Scripturas libenter audiunt in Ecclesia, vel apud se legunt, vel quoquo moda didicerunt. Aaron frater ipsius Fuit, quem ordinavit etiam Priester. Et ibi quidem non videtur sacerdos esse, nisi Aaron. Therefore what was said to Moses was figure, not punishment. What punishment is death for an old man? What punishment is it for not having entered the land into which the unworthy entered? What was said to Aaron? He also died an old man and his sons succeeded him in the priesthood, since after his death his son Eleazar exercised the priesthood. So how did God take revenge on this one? Saint Samuel also died old, leaving his sons as his successors. I inquire what God avenged on these men, and humanly I cannot find it; But, since I know that the servants of God suffer, he took revenge on them every day. Read and see the revenges, and those of you who profit, endure the revenges. Every day they endured the contradictions of the people, every day they tolerated those who lived iniquitously and they were forced to live among those whose lives they reviled every day. This was revenge. He who perceives it as small still does not take advantage, because the injustice of others torments you the more the more you have distanced yourself from your own. When you are wheat, that is, good grass with good seed, child of the kingdom; When you begin to bear fruit, then the tares will appear to you. You will want to distance yourself from the evil ones and separate them all from the Church, but you will be prevented by the sentence of the Lord, which says: Let both grow until the time of harvest, lest it happen that, when you want to uproot the tares, you uproot the wheat together with them. By God's decree it will be necessary to forgive the tares, and due to the condition of a servant, live among the tares. You can't separate it; then you need to tolerate it. Quotidie patiebantur populos contradícentes, quotidie patiebantur inique vivos; et inter illos vivere cogebantur, quorum vitam quotidie reprehendebant. Haec erat vindicta. 1. Brothers, when you sang you heard the psalm. It is brief and clear. With this I give you some security so that you do not fear the work. However, let us consider carefully, because the more unencumbered we are, the more carefully we must investigate what the things that are clearly said mean, so that, as far as the Lord deigns to grant us, we may understand them spiritually. The voice of God, in whatever instrument it sounds, is the voice of God, and only His voice pleases His ear, since, when we speak, we only please Him when He speaks for us. 2 (v. l]. This psalm is of confession or praise, for this is what its title reads: Psalm of praise or confession. It consists of a few words loaded with great things. Let the seed germinate in our hearts and the granary be prepared for the harvest of the Lord. This psalm of praise commands and exhorts us to rejoice in God. But it does not exhort any particular corner of the earth to sing, or any single dwelling place, or congregation of men, But, as He knows that He has spread the blessing throughout the world, the whole earth demands joy.

4. I have to say what you know. Qui iubilat, he who rejoices, does not utter words, but utters a certain sound of wordless joy. Rejoicing is a voice of the soul immersed in joy, which, as far as it can, makes known the affection, but not the feeling of the one who perceives it. As man rejoices in this joy, unable to explain or imply the affection in words, he emits

certain sound of joy without words. In this way he manifests by the same sound that he is happy; But since he is filled with too much joy, he cannot explain the joy in words. They slide without any disturbance; the stars walk from east to west, determining the courses of the years; We will also observe the extension of the months and the prolongation of the hours. Also in man there is something common with the angels of God; not what is common to animals, such as living, hearing, seeing and similar things, but knowing God, which belongs only to the mind; For just as the eye distinguishes white and black, it discerns justice and injustice. In this entire review of creation, which we were able to briefly name and review in a general way, the soul asks itself: Who made all these things? Who created them? What are you among all of them? What are these things you considered? What are you who ponders them? Who is He who made not only the things that must be considered, but the considerer? Who is this? Say who it is; For you to say it, think of Him, since you can think something and perhaps you cannot say it; However, there is no way you can say what you cannot think. Then think of Him before you say who He is. So that you think of Him, draw near to Him, because when you want to see well, so that you can speak, you draw near and look, lest, seeing from afar, you be deceived. However, the human heart is promised the vision of God and is invited to cleanse the heart; The Scripture says this: before you see, prepare your heart so that you can see what you love. Come close to Him and you will be enlightened. So that you may draw near and be enlightened, you may dislike your own darkness. Condemn what you are so that you deserve to be what you are not. Destroy it in your heart and cleanse it; cast it out of your heart, in which He whom you want to see wants to dwell. in the field. The two who are in the field are the clerics; One of them will be taken and the other will be left. The good will be taken and the bad will be left. The two women who are grinding symbolize the town. Why is it said that they are grinding? Because, chained to the world, they are as if held by the millstone in the work of temporal things, and from there one will be taken and the other left. Which of them will be taken? The one who works well and attends to the needs of the servants of God and the need of the poor; The one who is faithful in praise and is firm in the joy of hope and gives herself completely to God, no longer wishes harm to anyone, and loves as much as she can, not only her friends but also her enemies, and knows no other woman besides hers, nor any other man besides hers, this one, then, will be taken while she is at the mill; but that which is of a different condition must be abandoned. Others, on the contrary, say: "We long for rest, we do not want to put up with anyone; we will separate ourselves from the people, since it is better for us to live in a certain peace." If you are looking for rest, you are looking for a bed to rest without any worry. Also from here one will be taken and another left. Let no one deceive you, brothers. If you do not want to be deceived and you want to love your brothers, know that every profession in the Church has false workers. I did not say that every man is false, but that in every profession there are false individuals. There are bad Christians, but there are also good ones. You see many bad people, because they are chaff and do not allow you to get close to the grain; There are grains there too; Get closer, palpate, remove, explore, apply the sieve of judgment. Faciens opera bona, attendens indigentiam servorum Dei, indigentiam pauperum, in confessione fidelis, in laetitia spei certa, vigilans ad Deum, nulli imprecans mala, diligens quantum potest, non solum amicos, sed etiam inimicos, praeter uxorem suam non sciens aliquam, praeter maritum suum non sciens aliquem; assumetur et de molendino: quae autem aliter fuerit, relinquetur. Intrate in conspectu eius, in exsultatione. Facile est exsultare foris; in conspectu Dei exsulta. Non valid language exsultet; conscientia exsultet. made by Him, and without Him nothing was made. Why do you rejoice, why are you arrogant? He made you other than yourselves, and he who made you suffered for you. However, you rejoice, you glorify and you are proud, as if they had been made by you. It is good for you that He who made you perfect you. He made us, and not we made us. We must not be conceited; We have all the good that we possess from our creator. What we have done to ourselves is worthy of condemnation; what He did in us, worthy of coronation. He made us, and not we made us. We are his people and sheep of his pasture. We are sheep and sheep, because the same sheep are one sheep. And what a loving shepherd we have! He leaves ninety-nine and goes down to look for one, and carries it on his shoulder redeemed with his blood. The Shepherd who once resurrected possessed the sheep, died without fear for a sheep. His people {we are} and sheep of his pasture. 16 [v.4.5]. Enter its doors with praise or confession. At the door is the beginning. Start with confession. Hence the psalm is titled confession or praise. Rejoice here. Confess that you were not made and praise Him by whom you were made. All your good flows from Him from whom by turning away you perpetrated evil. Enter its doors with praise or confession. Between the flock through the doors, do not be left outside at the mercy of the wolf. And how will it get in? For the confession. The door, that is, the beginning, be confession for you. Hence it is said in another psalm: Begin {to enter} the Lord with praise. What it says in this psalm, begin, it says in the one we discussed in this way: doors. Enter through its doors est quod exsultatis? quid est quod superbitis? Alius vos fecit; et qui vos fecit, ipse a vobis patitur. Sed vos sic vos iactatis et gloriamini, et extollitis, quasi a vobis ipsis facti sitis. Bonum est vobis ut qui fecit vos, perficiat vos. Ipse fecit nos, et non nos. Non debenmus superbire: totum bonum quod habemus, ab artifice nostro habemus; quod in nobis nos fecimus, inde damnamur; quod in nobis ille fecit, inde coronamur. Ipse fecit nos, et non nos. Nos autem populus eius, et oves pascuae eius. Oves et ovis: ipsae oves an ovis. Et quam amantissimum nostri pastorem habemus! Dimisit nonaginta novem, descendit quaerere unam, reportat in humeris suis (Le 15,4.5) redemptam sanguine suo.

Securus mortuus est pastor pro ove, qui resurgens possidet ovem. Nos autem populus eius, et oves pascuae eius. 16 [v.4.5]. Intrate in portas eius in confessione. In portis initium est; a confession incipite. Inde Psalmus in confessione, ibi iubilate. Confitemini vos non factos a vobis, laúdate eum a quo facti estis. Ab illo sit bonum tuum, a quo recedens fecisti malum tuum. Intrate in portas eius in confessione. Intret grex in portas, non foris remaneat ad lupos. Et quomodo intert? In confession. Porta, id est initium, confessio tibi sit. Unde in alio psalmo dicitur: Incipite Domino in confessione (Ps 146,7). Quod illie dicit, Incipite: hoc appellavit hic, portas: Intrate in portas eius in confessione. Et quid, cum iam intraverimus, non confitebi-

with praise or confessing. And? After having entered, shall we not confess? You always have to confess, you always have something you must confess. It is difficult for man to be so transformed in this life that something should not be found in him that must be censured. It is necessary that you censure yourself so that he who is to condemn you does not do so. Then, when you enter the courts, confess. When will there be no confession of sins? In that rest, when men become equal to angels. Notice what I said: "There will be no confession of sins." I did not say: "There will be no confession," for there will be a confession of praise. You must always confess that He is God, and you are His creature; that He is protector, and you are His protected. In Him, in a certain way, you must hide, as it was said: You will hide them in the secret of your face. In his court confess him with hymns. Confess him at the gates, and as soon as you enter, confess him with hymns in the court. The hymns are songs of praise. When you enter, censure yourself; after you have entered, praise him. Open to me the doors of 'justice,' he says in another psalm; and, entering through them, I will praise the Lord. Did he say, "When I am inside, I will not praise"? After having entered, he will also praise, he will also confess. What sins did our Lord Jesus Christ confess when he said: I confess to you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth? He confessed, praising him, not accusing himself. 17. Praise his name, for sweet is the Lord. Do not think that you will fail in praise. Your praise will be like food. The more you praise, the more strength you will acquire and the sweeter will be He Whom you praise. Praise his name, for sweet is the Lord. His mercy forever. Won't it leave mur? Semper confitere, semper habes quod confitearis. Difficile est in hac vita, ut sic homo mutetur, ut nihil inveniatur in eo quod reprehendatur: opus est ut tu te reprehendas, ne ilie reprehendat qui damnaturus est. Ergo et cum intraveris in atria, confitere. When non erit confessio peccatorum? In illa requie, in illa aequalitate Angelorum. Sed videte quid dixerim: Non erit confessio peccatorum. Non dixi, Non erit confessio: erit enim confessio laudis. Semper confiteberis, illum Deum, te creaturam; illum protectorem, te protectum.

In illo quodammodo absconditus eris, sicut dictum est, Abscondes eos in abscondito vultus tui (Ps 30,21). In atria eius in hymnis confitemini ei. In portis confitemini; et in atria cum intraveritis, confitemini in hymnis. Hymni laudes sunt. When you enter, he rebukes you; cum intraveris, illum lauda. Aperite mibi portas iustitiae, dicit in alio psalmo; ingrediens in eis confit Domino (Ps 117,19). Numquid dixit, Cum ingressus fuero, iam non confitebor? Etiam ingressus confitebitur. Quae enim peccata confitebatur Dominus noster Iesus Christus, quando ait: Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine caeli et terrae? (Mt 11:25). Illum laudans confitebatur, non se accusans. 17. Laúdate nomen eius, quia suavis est Dominus. Nolite putare quia deficitis in laudando. Laudatio vestra quasi manducado erit: quantum laudatis, tantum vires acquiritis, et tantum dulcecit quem laudatis. Laúdate nomen eius, quia suavis est Dominus. In aeternum mercy

1 [v. l]. What this hundredth psalm states in the first verse is what we must investigate throughout its text. I will sing mercy and judgment to you, oh Lord! No one promises impunity for the mercy of God, because there is also judgment, and no one, changed for the better, fears the judgment of God, since mercy preceded. When men sometimes judge, carried away by mercy, they act against justice; It seems to them that they have mercy, but they lack judgment. Other times, eius. Non enim cum te liberaverit, desinet esse misericors: et ut protegat semper in aeternam vitam, misericordiae eius est. In aeternum ergo misericordia eius, et usque in generationem et generationem veritas eius. Aut omnem generationem accipe quod dictum est, in generationem et generationem; aut in duabus generationibus, unam terrenam, alteram caelestem. Hic est generatio una quae parit mortals; alter quae parit aeternos. Veritas eius et hic est, et ibi. Noli putare quia hic non est veritas eius: si non hic esset veritas eius, non diceret in alio psalmo: Veritas de terra orta est (Ps 84,12); nec ipsa Veritas diceret, Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem saeculi (Mt 28:20). PSALMUS SERMO

1 [v.l.]. Psalmus iste centesimus quod habet in primo versu, hoc in toto eius corpore quaerere debenmus. Misericordiam et iudicium sang tibi, Domine. Nemo sibi ad impunitatem blandiatur of mercy Dei; quia est et iudicium: et nemo in melius commutatus exhorreat iudicium Dei; quia praecedit mercy. Homines enim quando iudicant, aliquando victi misericordia, faciunt contra iustitiam; et videtur in eis esse misericordia, et non esse iudicium; aliquando vero tigidum volentes te-
Ennarrations on the Psalms

Wanting to be too upright in judgment, they abandon mercy. God, on the contrary, in the goodness of mercy does not abandon judgment, nor does he abandon the goodness of mercy in judging severely. You see that, if we distinguish the time of these two things: mercy and judgment, perhaps not without reason they maintain a certain order of priority in the text, since it was not said "judgment and mercy", but mercy and judgment; Perhaps, if we distinguish, I repeat, the time of these two things, perhaps we will find that now is the time of mercy, and the time to come is that of judgment. How does the time of mercy precede? Above all, set your sights on God so that you may imitate the Father in whatever He grants you. We do not arrogantly say that we should imitate our Father, since the Lord Himself, the only Son of God, exhorts us to this, saying: Be like your heavenly Father. When he says: Love your enemies, pray for those who persecute you, he adds: that you may be children of your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and rains on the righteous and the wicked. Here you have mercy. When you see the righteous and the wicked who contemplate the same sun, who perceive the same light, who drink from the same fountains, who are satisfied with the same rain, who are satisfied with the same fruits of the earth, who breathe the same air, who possess identical worldly goods, do not consider God unjust, who gives these things equally to the righteous and the wicked. It is the time of mercy; not yet from the trial. Well, if God did not first forgive us through mercy, He would not find something to crown with judgment. Then, nere iudicium, perdunt Misericordiam. Deus autem nec in Bonitate Misericordiae perdit iudicii Severitatem, nec in Judicando cum Severitate Amittit Misericordiae Bonitatem. Ecce si temporibus distinguamus haec duo, misericordiam et iudicium; forte enim non sine causa ipso ordine posita sunt, ut non diceret, Iudicium et misericordium, sed, misericordiam et iudicium: si ergo per tempora distinguamus haec duo, forte invenimus moda tempus esse misericiae, futurum autem tempus iudicii. How is primo tempus misericordiae?

Primo in Deoconsider, ut et tu quantum ipse tibí donaverit, imiteris Patrem. Ñeque enim arroganter dicimus, Patrem nostrum we will have to imitate; quandoquidem Dominus ipse unicus Dei Filius ad hoc nos hortatur, they say: Estofe sicut Pater vester caelestis. Cum diceret, Diligite inimicos vestros, orate pro eis qui vos persequuntur: ut sitis, inquit, filii Patris vestri qui in caelis est; qui solem suum facit oriri super bonds et malo, et pluit super iustos et iniustos (Mt 5,48.44.45). Ecce mercy. Quando vides iustos et iniustos eumdem solem intueri, eamdem luzem capere, eosdem fontes bibere, eadem pluvia saginari, iisdem fructibus terrae repleri, similiter aerem istum ducere, habere aequaliter bona mundi; noli putare iniustum esse Deum, qui dat ista aequaliter et iustis et iniustis. Misericordiae tempus est, nondum iudicii. Ñisi enim primo Deus per misericordiam parceret, non iiweniret quos per iudicium

When the patience of God draws sinners to penance, it is the time of mercy. 2. Hear the Apostle distinguish both times and you distinguish them. Do you think that you can escape the judgment of God, O man, that you judge those who do such things, and you do the same? Attend. He saw himself. But who is he saying this to? He does not say it to a single man, but to this class of men; It was seen in this class of men that they daily perpetrated many evil acts and that, nevertheless, they lived and that no harm came to them; and for this reason he thought either that God slept, or that He did not care about human things, or that He loved the evil actions of men. For the same reason, the Apostle removes this thought from the hearts of those who understand well. Well what does it say? Do you think that you have to escape the judgment of God, O man, that you judge those who do such things, and you do the same? And as if to say: "Why do I do so many evil works every day and no evil befalls me?", he then declares to him that it is the time of mercy by saying: Or do you despise the richness of his goodness, his patience and his long-suffering? Certainly because he despised this he made him solicitous, saying immediately: Don't you know that the kindness of God moves you to penitence? Here is the time of mercy. However, lest he think that this would last forever, he sees how it terrifies him. But you who have already heard the time of mercy in those words: Mercy and judgment I will sing to you, oh Lord! Listen now to the time of judgment. "You," he says, "according to the hardness of your heart and your impenitent spirit, store up wrath for the day of wrath and coronaret. Est ergo misericordiae tempus, quando patientia Dei ad poenitentiam adducit peccantes. 2. Audi Apostolum distinguishentem utrumque tempus, et distinguishes et tu: Existimas autem, inquit, o homo qui iudicas eos qui faciunt ea, et eadem agís, quoniam tu effugies iudicium Dei? Intend it. Videbat enim se (sed cui hoc dicit? Non enim vmi homíni dicit, sed generi hominum tali), videbat se committere fines mala quotidie, et tamen vivere, nihil mali sibi contingere; et putabat aut will sleep Deum, aut tes humanos non attendere, aut amare facta hominum mala.

Tollit istam cogitationem de corde, sed bene intelligentibus. Quid ergo ait? Existimas, o homo qui judicas eos qui talia agunt, et facis ea, quoniam tu effugies iudicium Dei? Et quasi diceret, Quare fació tanta mala quotidie, et nihil mali mihi contingit? secutus ostendit illi tempus misericordiae: An divitias benignitatis, et patientiae, et longanimitatis eius contemnis? Et veré quia hoc contemnebat; sed fecit illum sollicitum. Ignoras, inquit, quoniam benignitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Ecce tempus misericordiae. Ne autem hoc ille semper putaret futurum, quomodo secutus eum terruit? Tu autem (iam tempus iudicii audi; audisti tempus misericordiae, propter, Misericordiam et iudicium cantabo tibi, Domine): tu autem, inquit, secundum duritiam cordis tui et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis iusti iudicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum S.Ag.

the manifestation of the just judgment of God, which will give each person the payment of their works. Here you are: Mercy and judgment I will sing to you, oh Lord! He was frightened by the trial. But is it only the judgment of God that is to be feared and not loved? We must fear the bad because of the penalty, but we must love the good in view of the reward. Just as the Apostle frightened the wicked by the testimony I commemorated, so he hears hope among the good regarding the judgment. He sets himself out as an example, and thus exposes and declares in himself the time of mercy. If he had not found the time of mercy, how would he have found the time of judgment? It was blasphemous, persecuting, disastrous. Well, remembering the time of mercy, in which we now find ourselves, he says this: I who first judged blasphemous, persecuting and fatal; but I found mercy. Maybe only he got mercy? Hear how he encourages us: May Christ Jesus first manifest all long-suffering in me, serving as an example to all those who would believe in Him for eternal life. What does long-suffering mean in me? Let every sinner and wicked man see how Paul received forgiveness and not despair of himself. See how he manifested himself and how he encouraged others. When? In the time of mercy. Also listen to what he says about the good in the time of judgment, also speaking about himself and others. First he got mercy. Because? Because he was blasphemous, persecuting and impious. The Lord came to forgive Paul, but not to give him what he deserved; because, if he had wanted to give him his pay, what would he have found that could reward him other than the punishment

and of the torture? He did not want to repay the punishment, but rather to give him grace. Hear also how he who gave has the Lord as his debtor. He found the Lord a giver in the time of mercy, but he is a debtor in the time of judgment. See how Saint Paul himself says it: I am already beginning to be sacrificed and the time of my death is near; I fought the good fight, I finished the race, I kept the faith. This happened in the time of mercy. Hear him now speak of the time of judgment: Finally, the crown of righteousness remains for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will reward me on that day. He did not say: "Medará", but: He will reward me. When he gave he was merciful, when he gave back he was a judge, for mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord! Condoning the sins, he became a debtor for the reward. I obtained mercy, the Lord being first merciful; Then the palm of justice will reward me. Why will he give back? Because he is a just judge. And why is he a just judge? Because I fought the good fight, I finished the race and I kept the faith. And since it is fair, it cannot but reward these things. Now the Lord found these things to crown. But first, what had he found? First I was blasphemous, persecuting and impious. These he condoned, those he crowned. He condoned these in the time of mercy and crowned those in the time of judgment, because I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord! But perhaps only Paul deserved this? Just as I said that he frightened with that testimony, so I also say that he encouraged with this, since, having said: The Lord, the righteous judge, will reward me on that day, he adds: And not only to me, but to all those who love his appearance and his kingdom.

opera sua (Rom 2,3-6). Ecce, Misericordiam et iudicium cantabo tibi, Domine. Sed minatus est de iudicio: numquid ideo iudicium Dei tantummodo formidandum est, et non amandum? Formidandum malis propter poenam, amandum bonis propter coronam. Quia ergo terruit bad Apostolus in hoc testimony quod commemoravi, audi ubi spem dat bonis de iudicio. Seipsum ponit, et dicit, et ostendit et ipse in se tempus misericordiae. Quia nisi et ipse inveniret tempus misericorde, qualem illum inveniret iudicium? Blasphemum, persecutorem, iniuriosum. Sic enim dicit, et commendat tempus misericordiae, in quo moda sumus: Qui prius, inquit, fue blasphemus, et persecutor, et iniuriosus; sed mercym consecutus sum. Sed forte ipse solus consecutus est misericordion? Audi quomodo nos erigat: Ut in me, inquit, ostenderet Christus lesas omnem longanimitatem, ad informationem eorum qui credituri sunt Mi in vitam aetemam (1 Tim 1,13.16). Quid est, in me ostenderet longanimitatem? Ut unusquisque peccator et sceleratus videret quia Paulus accepit veniam, et non de se desperaret. Ecce ostendit se, erexit et alios. Ubi? In tempore misericordiae. Audi in tempore iudicii quid dicat de bonis, iterum dices de se et de alus. Primo Misericordiam Consecutus Est. Quare? Quia fuet blasphemus, et persecutor, et iniuriosus. Venit Dominus ut donaret Paulo, non ut redderet. Nam si reddere vellet, quid inveniret quod redderet peccatori, nisi poenam et supplicium? NoJuit

reddere poenam, sed donavit gratiam. Audi quia ille cui donavit, tenet Dominum etiam debitorem. Invenit eum donatorem tempore misericordiae, tenet debitorem tempore iudicii. Quomodo hoc dicit, videte. Ego enim iam immolor, dixit, et tempus resolutionis meae proximum est. Bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi. Hoc, tempore misericordiae, audi de iudicio. De caetero superest mihi corona iustitiae, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die iustus iudex. Non dixit, donat; thirst, reddet. When donabat, misericors erat; quando reddet, iudex erit: quia, Misericordiam et iudicium cantabo tibi, Domine. Sed donando delicta, fecit se coronae debitorem: ibi misericordiam consecutus sum. Misericors ergo Dominus primo, hic autem reddet mihi coronam iustitiae. Unde reddet? Quia iustus iudex est. Quare iustus iudex? Quia bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi. Ideo iustus non potest nisi coronare ista. Invenit enim ista quae coronaret: antea vero quid invenerat? Qui prius fue blasphemus et persecutor. Ista donavit, illa coronabit; donavit haec tempore misericordiae, coronabit illa tempore iudicii: quia, Misericordiam et iudicium cantabo tibi, Domine. Sed numquid solus Paulus id meruit? Hoc enim dixeram, quomodo in illo testimony terruit, sic in isto erexit. Cum dixisset, Reddet mihi Dominus in illo die iustus iudex: non solum mihi, inquit, sed omnibus qui diligunt manifestationem et regnum eius (2 Tim 4,6-8).

3. Then, brothers, so that we have time for mercy, let us not abandon ourselves, let us not flatter ourselves, let us not say: "God always forgives. I did this yesterday, and God forgave me; then I will do it also tomorrow, and he will forgive me." Thus you attend to mercy and do not fear judgment. If you want to sing mercy and judgment, understand that he forgives so that you correct yourself, but not so that you remain in iniquity. Do not want to store up anger for the day of wrath and the manifestation of God's righteous judgment. In another psalm it is said that, in the time of mercy, God said to the sinner: "Why do you declare my righteousness and take my testament in your mouth? You hated discipline and cast my words behind your back. If you saw the thief, you ran with him, and you took part with the adulterers; you sat down and spoke evil of your brother, and you put a stumbling block against your mother's son. This you did, and I kept silent." See here the time of mercy. What does callé mean? Did I not correct it? No, otherwise I did not judge. For how is he who daily cries out for the Scripture, for the Gospel, for the preachers, silent? He was silent regarding the judgment, but not regarding the correction. You did these things, and I was silent. And because God was silent, that is, because he did not punish, what did the sinner say in his heart? Hear it. You suspected—the psalm continues——because of iniquity that I am like you. That is to say, it seemed unimportant to you to be wicked, and you believed the same to me. But after having shown him the time of mercy, he terrified him with that of judgment, since he added: I will prove you and set you before your face. You stand behind you, I will put you in front of you. Everyone who does not want to see their sins puts them behind their backs; but subtly examines those of others,

not out of jealousy, but out of envy; Therefore, wanting not to cure, but to censure, he forgets himself. Hence the Lord says to these: You see the speck in your brother's eye and you do not see the beam in your own. Then, as mercy and judgment are sung to us, while we work mercy, let us wait for judgment. We are the Body of Christ; Let's sing these things. Christ sings this; If only the Head sings, this song is the Lord's, it does not belong to us. On the contrary, if the total Christ sings, namely, the Head and the Body, be of his members, join yourself to Him by faith, by hope and charity, and thus you will sing in Him and in Him you will rejoice, because He also suffers in you: He hungers and thirsts in you and is troubled in you. He still dies in you, and you have already risen in Him. If He had not died in you, I would not have wanted to be forgiven in you for the persecutor when he said: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? Therefore, my brothers, Christ sings, but as you know; I continually commend you to Christ and I know that you are not unaware of these things. Our Lord Jesus Christ is the Word of God, through whom all things were made. This Word, in order to redeem us, became flesh and lived among us. He who is God over all things, a Son equal to the Father, became man so that, being God-Man, he would be a Mediator between men and God, and thus reconcile those who are far away, unite those who are separated, call those who are disowned, and accompany pilgrims. For this he became a man. Then he became Head of the Church and has a body and members. Look at its members. Quia in tempore misericordiae in alio psalmo dicitur: "Peccatori autem dixit Deus, Utquid tu enarras iustificationes meas, et assumis testamentum meum per os tuum? Tu vero odisti disciplinam, et abiecisti sermones meos post te: si videbas furem, concurrebas ei, et cum moechis portionem tuam ponebas; sedens adversus fratrem tuum detrahebas, et adversus filium matris tuae ponebas scandalum. Vide tempus Misericordiae. What is it, tacui? Numquid, Non corripui? Sed, Non judicavi. Quomodo enim tacet qui quoddie clamat in Scripturis, in Gospel, in praedicatoribus suis? Tacui a supply, not a verb. Haec fecisti, et tacui. Et quia tacuit Deus, id est, non vindicavit: quid sibi dixit in corde peccator? Audi: Suspicatus es, inquit, iniquitatem, quod ero tibi similis. Id est, parum est quia your talis eras; et me talem putasti. Et cum ostendisset illi tempus misericordiae, terruit de tempore iudicii: Arguam te, et statuam te ante faciem tuam (Ps 49,16-21). You put yourself after you, ego puts you before you. Omnis enim

qui non vult videre peccata sua, post dorsum se ponit, et aliorum peecata acute attendit, non per diligentiam, sed per invidentiam; non volens sanare, sed aecusare: se autem obliviscitur. Unde talibus Dominus dicit, Stipulam in oculo fratris tui vides, et trabem in oculo tuo non vides (Mt 7,3) - Quia ergo misericordia et iudicium cantatur nobis, et nos facientes misericordiam securi exspectemus iudicium: et simus in corpore ipsius, et nos cantemus ea. Cantat enim hoc Christus: si solum caput cantat, a Domino est canticum hoc, ad nos non pertinet; si autem totus Christus, id est caput et corpus eius, esto in membris eius, adhaere illi per fidern, et per spem, et per charitatem; And in illo you sing, in illo you exult: quia et ipse in te laborat, in te sitit, in te esurit et tribulatur. Ule in te adhuc morituí, et tu in illo iam resurrecti. Nam si non in te moreretur, nollet in te sibi parci a persecutor, cum diceret: Sanie, Saule, quid persecute me? (Acts 9,4). Ergo, fratres mei, Christus cantat; sed quomodo, nostis: Christum assidue commendavimus vobis; et scio quia rudia vobis non sunt. Dominus Christus Verbum Dei est, per quod facta sunt omnia. Hoc Verbum ut tedimeret nos, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (lo 1,3.14): factus est homo Deus super omnia, Filius Dei aequalis Patri; ad hoc homo factus est, ut Deus homo mediator esset inter nomines et Deum, et reconcileret longe pósitos, et coniungetet separat, et revokeret alienaros, et reduceret petegtinos; ad hoc factus est homo. Factus est ergo caput Ecclesiae, habet et corpus et membra. Quaere membra ipsius, moda gemunt per universum orbem terrarum:

graced Who makes unfortunates? He who commits violence or perpetrates insidiousness, he who takes away what belongs to others, oppresses the poor, steals, disturbs the peace of marriages, is a slanderer and tries with a perverse will to infer to men some evil for which they may grieve. Who abandons the unfortunate? He who sees the poor person who needs some help and, having a way to help him, despises him, passes by and turns his heart away from him. If this man were such that he no longer needed mercy, yet he would be arrogant if he abandoned this unfortunate man, since he is still established in the tribulation of the flesh, not knowing what may happen to him tomorrow, and, nevertheless, he despises the tears of the unfortunate. This one is not innocent. Who is innocent? He who, by not harming others, does not harm himself either, because he who harms himself is not innocent. Someone says: "Look, I stole no one, I oppressed no one; I will treat myself well of my property, of my fair work; I want to celebrate a splendid banquet, I want to spend as much as I please, drink with those I desire as much as I please. Who did I steal from? Who did I oppress? Who complained about me?" He appears innocent. But if he ruins himself, if he destroys the temple of God in himself, how do you expect him to show mercy to others and forgive the unfortunate? Can he who is cruel to himself be merciful to a stranger? All justice comes down to a single word: innocence. He who loves iniquity hates his soul, says another psalm. When he loved iniquity, he thought that he did some harm to others; but see if it harmed others, since the psalmist says: He who loves iniquity hates his soul. Then firstly one perjulentias vel insidias, rapit res alienas, opprimit pauperes, furatur, coniugia aliena sollicitat, calumniosus est, vult inferre hominibus quo doleant, studio malevolentiae. Quis est qui deserit miseros:1 Qui videt inopem aliquo auxilio egentem, et cum habeat quomodo praestet, contemnit, despícit, alienat cor suum. Quod si iam omnino talis esset, ut non opus haberet aliqua mercy; superbus esset, si desereret miserum; adhuc in tribulatione carnis constitutus est, nesciens quid sibi possit eras accidere, et despicit lacrymas miserorum; he is not innocent. Sed quis est innocens?

God wants. Attend. An individual prays so that something does not happen to him; He prays and is not prevented. Pray as much as you can. But, if something happens to you against your will, submit to the will of God, do not oppose the sublime will. For the Lord himself, making our weakness known in Himself, declared it thus when He was close to the passion: My soul is sad until death. Without a doubt, he who had the power to give life and take it up again did not fear death. Saint Paul, soldier and servant of Christ, also exclaims: I fought the good fight, I finished the race, I kept the faith; Furthermore, the crown of righteousness is reserved for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will reward me on that day. He rejoices because he must die, and is his Lord, his Emperor, sad because he is close to death? Is the servant then better than the Lord? What shall we say about what the Lord himself says: It is enough for the servant to be like his Lord, for the disciple to be like his Master? Is Saint Paul encouraged by the imminence of death, and is the Lord sad? I desire—he says—to die and be with Christ. He rejoices in death to be with Christ, and Christ himself, with whom Saint Paul must rejoice by being with Him, is he sad? What was that voice but the sound of our weakness? Many weak people are still saddened by future death; But, nevertheless, having a right heart, avoid death if you can, and if you cannot, say what the Lord said, not for yourselves, but for us. What did he say? Father, if it is possible, pass this chalice from me. Here you have declared the human will. Now see the upright heart: However, let not be done what I want, but what you want, O Father! Then, if the right heart goes

In pursuit of God's will, the depraved person opposes Him. Something adverse happens to him and he exclaims: "O God, what have I done to you? What evil have I committed? In what have I sinned?" He considers himself to be just, and God to be unjust. What a depraved man! He thinks it is not enough to be crooked, and he thinks that the rule is crooked. Correct yourself and you will find what is right, from which you turned away. God is just, you are unjust; You are perverse, because you say that man is just, and God is unjust. What man do you call righteous? To yourself, because when you say: "What did I do to you?", you consider yourself righteous. Without a doubt, God will answer you: "You say the truth, because you did nothing to me; you did it to yourself. If you had done something to me, you would have done good. Everything good that is done, is done to me, because it is done because of my commandment. On the contrary, everything bad that is done is done for you, not for me, since the evil person does not do anything except for himself, since I do not command evil." When you come across this kind of men, brothers, rebuke, argue, correct, do not consent, so that you may say: No depraved heart joined me. 7. When the wicked departed from me, he did not know. What does it mean I didn't know? I did not approve, I did not praise, I did not please. We find in Scripture that sometimes it is said to know by pleasing. What is hidden from God, my brothers? Does he know the righteous and not the unrighteous? What do you think I ignore? I'm not saying what you do, but what you think He ignores; And I'm not saying what you think, but what you should think that He doesn't foresee. God knows all things, and yet at the end, that is, at the hour of judgment, after mercy, he says of certain individuals:

Petat quantum potest: sed contra voluntatem ipsius evenit aliquid; subiungat se voluntati Dei, non resistat voluntati magnae. Quia et ipse Dominus sic illud exponit: ostendens infirmitatem nostrara in se, quando passurus erat, ait, Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Non enim veré ille timebat mortem, qui potestatem habebatponerdi animam suam, et potestatem habebat iterum sumendi eam (lo 10,18). Et Paulus apostolus miles ipsius, servus ipsius clamat: Bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi; de caetero reposita est mihi corona iustitiae, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die tustús iudex. Exsukat quia mounts est; et Dominus eius et Imperator eius tristis est, quia moriturus est! Ergo melior servus quam Dominus? Et ubi est quod ait ipse Dominus: Sufficit servo ut sit sicut dominus eius; sufficit disciple ut sit sicut magister eius? (Mt 10:25). Ecce fortis est Paulus ventura morte, et Dominus tristis est! Optabam, inquit, dissolvi, et esse cum Christo (Phil 1,23). Gaudet, quia dissolvitur, ut sit cum Christo; et ipse Christus tristis est, cum quo iste futurum se esse laetatur! Sed quid erat illa vox, nisi sonus infirmitatis nostrae? Multi adhuc infirmi contristantur future morte: sed habeant rectum cor; vitent mortem, quantum possunt; sed si non possunt, dicant quod ipse Dominus non propter se, sed propter nos dixit. Quid enim dixit? Pater, si fieri potest, transeat a me calix iste. Ecce habes voluntatem humanom expressam; vide iam rectum cor: Verum, non quod ego flew, sed quod tu vis, Pater (Mt 26,38.39). On that day many will come and say to me: "Lord, in your name we have cast out demons, in your name we performed many miracles, in your name we have eaten and drunk"; and I will say to them, "Depart from me, you workers of iniquity; I do not know you." Do you perhaps not know any of them? So what does it mean I don't know you? I do not see you in my rule or law. I know the rule or norm of my justice; you did not conform to it, you turned away from it, and you are crooked. That is why he also said here: I did not know. When the wicked departed from me, I did not know. What does it mean I didn't know? Perhaps that the wicked, when he comes face to face with a righteous man on a narrow path, says to himself what was written in the Book of Wisdom of Solomon: It is hard for us even to see him, and he changes his route so as not to see him whom he does not want to see? But how many wicked people there are, whom we see and who see us, who not only do not depart from us, but run towards us and sometimes wish that we sanction their own iniquities! This happens to us frequently. Then how come they separate? He who is unlike you departs from you. What does "depart from you" mean? He doesn't follow you. What does "not follow you" mean? He doesn't imitate you. Then, when the evildoer departs from me, that is, when the evildoer is unlike me, and does not want to follow in my footsteps, and does not want to live like me, he proposes me to him as a model, (but I will say): I did not know. What does it mean I didn't know? That he did not approve, not that he ignored. 8 [v.5]. He persecuted those who underhandedly accused their neighbors. Behold the good persecutor, not of man, but of tamen in fine, id est in iudicio post Misericordiam, of quibusdam dicit: "In illa die multi venturi sunt, et dicet, Domine, Domine, in nomine tuo daemonia eiecimus, in nomine tuo virtutes fines fecimus, in nomine tuo manducavimus et bibimus; et dicam illis, Discedite a me, operanii iniquitatis; non novi vos" (Mt 7,22 et 23). Ule non novit aliquem? Sed quid est, Non novi vos? In regula mea non vos agnosco. Novi enim regulam iustitiae meae: non illi congruitis, declinastis ab illa, distorti estis. Then, why do we observe that the Lord ate first with the proud? Note carefully that I do not say: "With the publicans and sinners", since these were humble. They knew about their illness and looked for a doctor. We see that he ate with the same proud Pharisees, since a certain proud man invited him; the one who was displeased when the sinful and famous woman in the city approached the feet of the Lord; For the purity of the Pharisees was such that they did not allow any wicked person to touch them. And, if any unclean person touched them in the slightest, they were horrified, lest the imperceptible contact would turn them unclean. For this reason, as soon as the sinner, well known in the city, came crying to the feet of the Lord, when the proud Pharisee saw her, he said in his heart: If this man were a prophet, he would know what woman is coming to his feet. How did she know that Christ did not know her if it were not because she believed that he did not know her, since he did not separate her from him? If he had been a prophet, he would have kept her away from him. The Lord not only knew the sinful woman, but also saw, as a doctor, the incurable wounds of that proud man. Well, upon perceiving his thoughts, to show him that he was arrogant, he said to him: Simon, I have something to tell you: There were two debtors of a lender; One owed him five hundred denarii, the other fifty; Not having the means to repay him, he forgave both of them. On this night God forgives sinners so as not to annihilate them; troubles them with temptations to correct them; He supports them in his city. But are we to believe that he will always tolerate it? If it is eternally a time of mercy, there will be no judgment; But if mercy and judgment I will sing to him, oh Lord, forgive now and then judge. When will he judge? When the night had passed. That is why he said: Early in the morning he killed all the sinners on earth. What does "early morning" mean? As the day approaches, the night passes. At dawn he killed all the sinners on earth. You see a man who lives badly: you tolerate him, because you don't know what it is, because it is at night, and you don't know if he who lives badly today will live well tomorrow, or if he who lives well today will live badly tomorrow. About the first part of Psalm 1 [v.l]. Behold, a poor man prays, and he does not pray in silence. It is advisable to listen to him and see who he is, lest it happen that perhaps he is the one about whom the Apostle says that he became poor for you, being rich, so that with his poverty you would become rich. But if it is He, how is he poor? Well, who doesn't see that he is rich? Why are men rich? I think for the gold, for the silver, for the family, for the estate. Well, all these things were made by Him. And what is richer than Him by whom riches were made, even those that are not true? For through Him other riches were also made: ingenuity, memory, customs, life, bodily health, sense, the conformation of the members; Without a doubt, when these things are well preserved, because of them even the poor are rich. Through Him other greater riches were also made: faith, piety, justice, charity, interficiet eos Christus in matutinis, et disperdet eos de civitate sua. Sed moda cum tempus misericordiae est, audiant eum. If there had been freedom to sin and forgiveness had been lacking, where would you be, where would you go? Without a doubt, it happened because of you that this poor man ate ashes as bread and mixed his drink with crying. Doesn't such a treat already delight you? And? "Thus men," he says, "increase sins in the hope of forgiveness." On the contrary, sins would increase with the desperation of forgiveness. Don't you see the wanton cruelty with which gladiators live? Where does this come from? That, considering themselves destined to be a victim of the sword, they want to satisfy lightness before shedding blood. Would you not also say this to yourself: "I am a sinner, a wicked man, a man who must be condemned, there is no hope of forgiveness. Why should I not do whatever I want, even if it is not permitted? Why should I not satisfy all my desires as much as I can, if after this life there remains nothing but torment?" Wouldn't you tell yourself this, and out of desperation would you become worse? Then he who promises you forgiveness rather corrects you and says: Prevaricators, enter into the heart; and also: I do not want the rmt-erte of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Without a doubt, with the offer of this port you lower the sails of iniquity, you change course, you sail towards justice and, hoping in life, you do not disdain medicine. Do not dislike God, as if by this promise of forgiveness he made sinners confident. So that men would not live worse because of despair, he promised the harbor of forgiveness; and so that through the hope of forgiveness they would not live worse, he established the uncertain day of death for men. Thus, by providentially determining both things, those who convert find a place in which they must be received, and those who are retarded or trusting find a reason for terror. In view of your anger and your indignation, because you lifted me up, you crushed me. This, Lord, is that anger of Yours against Adam. Anger with which we are all born, and, being born, we find ourselves attached to it; wrath arising from the spread of iniquity, wrath arising from the mass of sin, according to which the Apostle says: We were also once, by nature, children of wrath, like the rest. From here the Lord also says: The wrath of God will remain on him who did not believe in the only begotten Son of God. He did not say, "The wrath of God will come upon him," but it will remain upon him, because that with which he was born has not been taken away. What does this sentence mean and what does it mean: Because you lifted me up, you smashed me?, since it does not say: "Because you lifted me up and smashed me," but: Because you lifted me up, you smashed me. That is, you crashed me because you lifted me up. Where does this come from? (Let's see it.) Man was constituted in honor of being created in the image of God. Raised to this dignity, raised terreantur. Manduca cinerem velut panem, et fletum tuum cum potu misce; per hoc convivium venies ad mensam Dei. Noli hope; promissa est indulgentia tibi. Deo gratias, inquit, quia promissa est; teneo promissum Dei. Ergo iam bene vive. Cras, inquit, bene vivam. Indulgentiam tibi Deus promisit; crastinum diem tibi nemo promisit. From the dust, exalted on earth, he received the rational soul, and thus he took precedence, by the excellence of his reason, over all beasts, animals, birds and fish. Well, which of these has intelligence? None of them were made in the image of God. And as none of them possesses this dignity, so none of them possesses this misery. What animal cries for sin? What bird fears eternal fire? Just as he does not participate in any way in the blessed life, he does not feel sorry for miseries. However, man, who was created to possess eternal life if he lived well, will go to a miserable life for living badly. Then because you lifted me up, you crashed me. Therefore, sorrow accompanies me, because you granted me free will. Well, if you had not given me free will and, due to reason, had not created me in a better condition than the beasts, just condemnation would not accompany me, a sinner. Then by free will you lifted me up and by righteous judgment you crashed me. 12 [v. 12]. My days passed like a shadow. Your days might not have passed if you had not turned away from the true day. You set aside and received the days that pass. Why do you marvel that your days have become like you? They are days that pass, because you have gone astray; days of smoke, because you were puffed up. Previously he said: My days vanished like smoke; Now he says: My days passed like a shadow. In this shadow the day must be recognized, in this shadow the light must be seen, so that it is not said later with belated and fruitless repentance: What good did pride do to us and what did pride bring us? ipsius vivacitate omnibus bestiis, pecoribus, volatilibus, piscibus (Gen 1:26). Quid enim horum habet intelligentiae rationem? Quia nullum horum factum est ad imaginem Dei. Quomodo nullum horum habet hunc honorem, sic nullum horum habet hanc miseriam. Quod enim pecus plangit de peccato? quae avis timet gehennam ignis aeterni? Quia nulla ei participatio beatae vitae, nulli stimuli miseriarum. Homo autem, quia factus est qui sit in beata vita, si bene vixerit; ideo erit in misera vita, quia male vixit.

Then run now, because he attended to the prayer of the humble and did not despise his request. 19 [v.19.20]. Let these things be written for the coming generation. When these things were recorded, those among whom they were written were not discovered. Well, they were written to prophesy the New Testament among men who lived by the Old Testament. Yet God had given them the Old Testament and placed his people in the promised land. But since your memorial is for generation and generation, not of the wicked, but of the righteous, hence the Old Testament belongs to one generation and the New to the other. And as it announces to the New Testament what was prophesied: Let these things be written for the generation to come, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord, not the people already created, but the one that will be created, what is clearer, my brothers, than the preaching that is made here of the creature, of which the Apostle says: Therefore, if anyone is already a new creation in Christ, the old things have already passed away; See that all things have become new, and all things come from God? 2 fv.20-22}. From heaven the Lord looked upon the earth to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to free the children of those condemned to death. We find that it is said in another psalm: Enter into your presence the groaning of the prisoners, and it is said precisely in the place in which we understood that the martyrs were being spoken of. But how were the martyrs put in irons? Were they not chained rather than shackled? We know that, when the holy martyrs of God were brought before the judges, traveling through the provinces, they were sent to them in chains; but we do not know that they were shackled. Here are proclaimed the fetters of God's teaching and of his fear, about which it was said: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God. Because of this fear, the servants of Goddess did not fear those who kill the body and cannot kill the soul, since they feared him who has the power to kill the body and the soul and send them to hell. If the martyrs had not been bound by the shackles of this fear, how would they have endured all those cruelties and hardships on the part of their persecutors, when they were left free to do what they were ordered, and thus avoid what they suffered? But God had tied them temporarily with these fetters, undoubtedly cruel and laborious, which had to be tolerated in attention to the promises of Him Whom it is said: By the words of your lips, I kept your painful ways. Certainly one must groan while in these fetters in order to implore God's mercy. Hence the martyrs say in another psalm: Enter into your presence the groaning of those in chains. For such fetters are not to be avoided for wanting the pernicious freedom and sweetness of 2 [v.20-22]. Dominus de cáelo in terram prospexit, ut audiret gemitum compeditorum, ut solvat filias mortificatorum. Invenimus in alio psalrao dictum, Intret in conspectum tuum gemitus compeditorum (Ps 78,11); et in eo loco dictum, ubi vox martyrum intelligebatur. Unde martyres compediti? Nonne catenati potiusquam compediti? Ducts enim sanctos Dei martyres post iudíces, per circumeuntes provinces, in catenas novimus missos; in compedes autem non novimus. Agnoscuntur et compedes disciplinae Dei et timoris eius, de quo dictum est: Initium sapientiae titnor Domini (Eccli 1,16).

Per hunc enim timorem non timuerunt servi Dei eos qui corpus occidunt, animam autem non possunt occidere; quia eum timebant qui habet potestatem et Corpus et animam occidere in gehennam ignis (Mt 10,28). Nisi enim cornpedibus timoris huius ligad essent martyres, quando illa omnia dura et molesta sustinerent a persecutoribus suis, cum eis liberum fuerit faceré quod cogebantur, et evadere quod patiebantur? Sed alligaverat eos Deus istis cornpedibus, duris quidem et molestis ad tempus, sed tolerandis propter promissa eius, cui dicitur: Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi fias duras (Ps 16,4). Gemendum quidem est in his cornpedibus ad impetrandam misericordiam Dei; unde vox martyrum est in alio psalmo, Intret in conspectum tuum gemitus compeditorum: non tamen Evitandae sunt such compedes, ut appetatur perniciosa libertas, et temporalis vitae brevisque

short and temporary life, which is followed by perpetual bitterness. Therefore, so that we do not reject the fetters of wisdom, the Scripture speaks to us in this way: Hear, my son, and receive my decree and do not reject my advice: put your foot and your neck into its collar; Subdue your shoulder, and carry wisdom, and do not hate its chains. Draw near to her with all your heart and keep her ways with all your strength. Inquire and seek, and it will be made known to you; and, once achieved, do not abandon it. Because in the last days you will find rest in it and it will become joy for you; and his fetters will serve as protection for your fortress, and his necklace as a stole of glory. She has sparkles of gold, and her chains, filaments of hyacinth. You will put it on as a stole of glory and put it on yourself as a crown of rejoicing. Then let those in chains cry out while they are chained by the discipline of God, in which the martyrs were exercised. For the crickets will break and fly away, and then the crickets themselves will become an ornament. This happened with the martyrs. Well, what did the persecutors do by killing but releasing the fetters and turning them into crowns? 3. Since they are condemned to death, who are their children? Us. When are we released? When we tell him: You broke my ties. To you I will sacrifice a host of praise. 1. If you remember, the day before yesterday you were abundantly fed. But since you left eagerly even after the long sermon, I have not thought it appropriate to defraud your holiness with today's debt; Therefore, let today's debt be your debt, and the day before yesterday's gain. The psalm read is almost entirely composed of figures and mysteries, and needs not only our attention, but also yours, and not a small one, even though all the things it narrates can also be piously taken literally. In it are enumerated, if not all, then many works of God, which are known to all who contemplate them, who know that by these that were made and are seen they can see with the mind the invisible ones of God. We see, then, the immense fabric of the world constituted by the sky and the earth and all the things they contain. Because of the beauty and greatness of this factory, we love, although we do not yet see, the excellent magnificence and beauty of its Artificer, since He who cannot yet be contemplated by the purity of our heart did not cease to put before our eyes his works,^ so that, seeing what we can see, we love him who we cannot yet see, and thus, because of his love, we can see him at some time. However, of all the things recorded in the psalm, the spiritual meaning must also be investigated. PSALMUS SERMO

Aren't you always great? Aren't you always powerful? Are you imperfect, and therefore you grow? Do you decline, so that you sometimes diminish? Without a doubt you are great, and your greatness is everlasting, since it neither begins nor ceases to exist, nor does it begin with time nor suffer any detriment in the midst of it; It is immutable greatness. Then how did you become exceedingly great? Another psalm explains it to us, saying: Your knowledge has become great in me. If it is rightly said: Your knowledge {or knowledge) was great in me, it will equally be said: Lord, my God, you have become exceedingly great in me. But this still needs to be investigated. Does my God magnify himself in me? Then it becomes big on me. Let's attend. Daily prayer teaches us something about our health. Let your name be hallowed. Every day we ask, every day we pray that this be fulfilled. If anyone asks us: "What do you ask when you say that the name of God be sanctified? Congratulations are one thing and prayer is another. We congratulate ourselves for what is and pray that it is what it is not yet. So what does it mean to be your name hallowed? I did not say more than what the Apostle said when, speaking of the two sons of Abraham, he wrote that they are recorded allegorically. What is called an allegory is what sounds one way and means something different from what the words express. For example, Christ is called lamb. Is he a beast? He is called a lion. Is it perhaps fierce? It is called stone. Is he insensitive? It is called Mt. Is it elevation of land? Thus there are many things that sound one way and mean different things; This is called allegory. Whoever thinks that I used the word allegory, taking it from theatrical art, must also judge that the Lord used the word parable, taking it from the amphitheater. You understand what the city in which spectacles abound provides; In the field I would speak without worrying, because men there would not have known what allegory is, if they had not learned it in the Scripture of God. Then, by saying that allegory is a figure, we say that allegory is a figurative sacrament. And what are we to understand by what is said: Rise on the wings of the winds? We have said that in all righteousness the winds are figuratively taken for souls. What are the wings of the winds, that is, the wings of the souls? Those by which they rise high. Therefore the wings of souls are virtues, good works, right deeds. All these wings are reduced to two, just as all precepts are reduced to two. Anyone who loves God and his neighbor has his soul endowed with wings and flies with holy love towards the Lord with his wings free. On the contrary, everyone who is entangled in carnal love has the locum suum in scena involved. Non enim ego dixi quod Apostolus non dixit, cum de duobus filiis Abrahae diceret: Quae sunt, inquit, in allegoria (Gal 4,24). Allegoria dicitur, cum aliquid aliud videtur sonare in verbis, et aliud in intellectu significare. Quomodo dicitur agnus Christus (lo 1,29): numquid pecus? Leo Christus (Rev 5,5): numquid beast? Petra Christus (1 Cor 10:4): numquid duritia? Mons Christus (Dan 2,35): numquid tumor terrae? Et sic fines aliud videntur sonare, aliud significare; et vocatur allegoria. Your charity remembers that I owe the exposition of the remainder of this psalm, and I do not need to excite your attention with some proem, since I see you hanging on my lips with the greatest interest in order to understand the prophetic mysteries. Therefore, I repeat, my speech does not need to excite the attention of those who have already been aroused by the spirit of God. Let us rather deal with what is urgent. They talked about the fountains that flow in the valleys and the waters that flow between the mountains. Up to this point it has already been explained. Let's start from here. 2 [v. l l ]. The psalm continues: All the beasts of the forest will drink. What will they drink? The waters that flow between the mountains. What will they drink? The spring that flows in the valleys. Who will drink? The beasts of the jungle. We certainly see in creation that the beasts of the forest drink the waters of the fountains and streams that flow between the mountains. But as it pleased God to hide his wisdom under the figure of such things, but not to deprive the scholars of it, but to close it to the negligent and open it to those who call, so it also pleased our God and Lord to exhort you for me so that in all the things that are narrated as if they were dealing with the corporeal and visible creation we may investigate something spiritual and hidden, with what we have found we will rejoice

1. Reliquarum partium psalmi huius pertractandarum debitores nos esse meminit Chantas Vestra. Non ergo opus est ut intentionem vestram aliquo proemio moveam. Video enim vos ad intelligenda sacramenta prophetica omni alacritate suspense; nec opus est ut attempts faciat sermo meus, quos iam fecit Spiritus Dei. Hoc potius agamus quod urget. De fontibus emissis in convallibus, et de aquis Inter medium montium pertranseuntibus iam dicrum est: sed hucusque dictum; hinc deinceps ordiamur. 2 [v.ll]. Sequitur enim: Potabunt omnes bestiae silvae. Quid potabunt? Aquas pertransentes inter medium montium. Quid potabunt? Sources emissos in convallibus. Et qui potabunt? Bestiae silvae. Videmus quidem hoc etiam in ista creatura, bestias silvae bibere de fontibus et de rivis inter montes currentibus: sed iam quoniam Deo placuit talium rerum figuris abscondere sapientiam suam, non auferre studiosis, sed claudere negligentibus, aperire pulsantibus; placuit etiam ipsi Domino Deo nostro ad hoc hortari vos per nos, ut in his omnibus, quae velut de corporali et de visibili creatura dicuntur, quaeramus aliquid spiritualiter absconditum, quo invento gaudeamus. Bestias silvae, Gentes intelligimus; et multis hoc locis Scriptura testatur. Be very evident

mos. By beasts of the forest we understand the Gentiles, since this is stated in many places in Scripture. In fact, two very obvious proofs are offered to us; The first, Noah's ark, which none of us doubts prefigured the Church, since all kinds of animals would not have been enclosed in it if all the Gentiles had not been symbolized in that bond of unity, unless we think that, if all these kinds of animals had perished at all by the flood, God would have lacked the power to command the earth to produce them, as it produced them first by His Word. Therefore the animals were not included in the ark either vainly or recklessly, nor because of any lack or weakness of God's power. Because later, when the time came, and we must add another very obvious testimony, when the time came for what was prefigured in the ark to be fulfilled in the Church, the apostle Saint Peter doubting that he would give the evangelical sacrament to the uncircumcised, in fact, not doubting, but believing that in no way should it be given to them, feeling hungry one day, as he wanted to eat, he went up to pray. This is well known to all who hear or read the Acts of the Apostles. As he was praying, then, that alienation or rapture of spirit came upon him, which the Greeks call ecstasy; That is to say, his mind was separated from the ordinary and bodily habit of seeing to contemplate a certain vision, detaching himself from what was present. Then he saw a container like a sheet descending from heaven, supported by the four corners, in which were found all kinds of animals, all kinds of beasts, and immediately a voice was heard saying: duo máxime occurrunt documenta, quod in arca Noe, qua nemo nostrum dubitat Ecclesiam esse praefiguratam, non includerentur omnia genera animalium (Gen 7,2.14), nisi in illa unitate compaginis omnes gentes signifícarentur: nisi forte putamus, si omnia talia penitus deluge delerentur, defuturam Fuisse Deo potestatem iubendi ut tetra ea produceret, sicut primo verbo eius produxerat (ib. 1,24). Non ergo frustration, non fear, non aliqua indigentia Dei vel inopia potestatís iussa sunt animalia illa in arca includi.

Nam posteaquam venit tempus (iam enim debenmus et alterum evidentissimum adiungere testimonium): cum ergo venit tempus, ut illud quod in arca erat praefiguratum, iam in Ecclesia compleretur, Petrus apostolus dubitans daré sacramentum evangelicum Gentibus incircumcisis; imo non dubitans, sed omnino dandum esse non putans, quodam die esuriens cum prandere vellet, ascendít ut oraret. Hoc in Actibus Apostolorum omnibus bene legentibus et bene audientibus notum est. Ulo igitur orante facta est illi mentís alienated, quam Graeci ecstasin dicunt: id est, aversa est mens eius a consuetudine corporali ad visum quemdam contemplandum, alienata a praesentibus. Tune vidit vas quoddam veluti linteum quatuor lineis submitti de cáelo, ubi erant omnia animalia, omnis generis bestiae; et sonuit ei vox: Petre, macta, et manduca. He, who had been instructed in the law, and who had grown up in the Jewish custom, and who retained the precept of God given by Moses and had faithfully kept it all his life, answered: Far be it from me, O Lord! For nothing common has ever entered my mouth. Those who learned ecclesiastical science know very well that the Jews and the law call what is unclean common. Then it was answered: What God has purified, do not call unclean. This happened three times, and immediately the container that was shown to him three times coming down from heaven disappeared. The container held at the four ends symbolized the earthly orb, divided into four parts; Scripture frequently lists these parts: the east, the west, the north, and the south. Since the entire world is called to the Gospel, four gospels were written for the same reason. The ternary sending of the vessel also means that the apostles were told: Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. From here we also derive, as you know, the duodenary number of the apostles. He did not want there to be twelve in vain. This number was so sacred that, in place of the one that fell, another could not be ordained. Why were there twelve apostles? Because there are four parts of the world, and the whole world was called to the Gospel; Hence four gospels were written and the entire world was called in the name of the Trinity to form the Church. Four, added three times, forms the number twelve. Therefore let us not marvel that all the beasts of the jungle drink of those waters that flow between the mountains, of that apostolic doctrine that flows in their midst in attention to the unity of communion. All the beasts were in the ark, all vitam suam fideliter custodierat, responded: Absit a me, Domine; nunquam commune aliquid intravit in os meum. Commune autem immundum dici a Iudaeis et a Lege, bene noverunt qui ecclesiasticas litteras didicerunt. Et vox ad illum: Quae Deus mundavit, tu immunda ne dixeris. Hoc autem factum est ter, et ablatus est ille discus qui demonstrabatur ter de cáelo submissus (Acts 10,9-16). Discus qui quatuor lineis continebatur, orbis terrarum erat in quatuor partibus.

Has four parts saepe Scriptura commemorat, orientem et occidentem, aquilonem et meridiem. Ideo quia totus orbis per Evangelium vocabatur, quatuor Evangelia conscripta sunt. Ter autem submissum de cáelo vas hoc significat, quia dictum est Apostolis: Ite, baptízate omnes gentes in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti (Mt 28,19). Inde colligitur, sicut iam nostis, duodenarius etiam numerus discipulorum. Non enim frustration duodecim habere voluit; et ita numerus ille sacratus est, ut in locum unius qui ceciderat, non posset nisi alter ordinari. Quare duodecim Apostoli? Quia enim quatuor sunt orbis parts, et totus orbis in Evangelio vocabatur, unde quatuor Evangelia conscripta sunt, et totus orbis in nomine Trinitatis vocatur, ut congregetur Ecclesia: quatuor ter ducta, duodecim fiunt. The onagers will drink it in their thirst. He calls certain large beasts onagers. Who doesn't know that onagers are wild asses? Then he calls certain untamed ones great. The Gentiles did not know the yoke of the law. Countless people lived with proud boasting, wandering in their customs as in the desert. They are all certainly beasts, but they were called onagers to highlight their greatness. All of these will drink them in their thirst, because the waters also flow for them. From here the hare drinks, from here the wild onager; mundus per eum jactus est (lo 1,1.10). Tale verbum contemplaturi sumus. Apparebit enim Deus deorum in Sion (Ps 83,8). Be hoc when? Post pilgrimagem finita via; si tamen post finitam viam non iudici tradamur, ut iudex mittat in carcerem. Be si finita via, sicut speramus, et optamus, et studemus, ad patriam venerimus, ibi contemplabimur quod semper laudabimus: nec illud deficiet quod nobis praesto est, nec nos qui fruimur; nec fastidiet qui manducaba, nec deficiet quod manducabit. Magna illa et mira contemplated erit.

The little hare and the big onager, the timid hare and the fierce onager, both drink from here, but each according to his thirst. Cui sonat Psalmus et dicat: Multum est ad me? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who feeds the flock and does not receive its milk? I am not saying this so that this can be fulfilled with me. I was, says the Apostle, certainly a soldier who forgave the provider's food; but, nevertheless, let the provider give food. To put it better, I will say: They are donkeys; and: You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes. You, he says, produce hay for the donkeys; and, as if expounding this, he adds: and grass for the service of men, so that you would understand that what he said before: You produce hay for the donkeys, he declared in this repetition. Since what was called hay above, he immediately called grass, and what he said about the donkeys, he expressed it by saying; for the service of men; then by obligation, not freely. So how is it that it is said: You were called to freedom? But listen to the same Apostle: Being free of all, I became a servant of all to win all. Well then, to those who said, You were called to freedom, what did he add? Do not turn freedom into an occasion of the flesh, but rather, out of charity, become servants of others. Those whom he made free, he makes servants, not by condition, but by the redemption of Christ; not out of necessity, but out of charity. Out of charity, he says, serve one another. We mutually serve Christ, he says, not the iumentis. "De fructu operum tuorum, inquit, saliatibur terra: produces fenum iumentis. Tu noli esse sterilis, produc fenum iumentis: si nolunt iumenta fenum tuum, non te tamen sterilem inveniant. Accipis spiritualia, redde carnalia: debita sunt militi, militi reddis; provincialis Christi es. Quis militat sais stipendiis unquam? quis plantat vineam, et de fructu eius non edit? quis pascit gregem, et de lacte eius non percipit?

Fuit quídam miles qui etiam provinciali donaret annonam: sed tamen reddat provincialis annonam. Ut autem hinc dicam potius; iumenta sunt: Bovi Crushantis os non infrenabis. Producens, inquit, fenum iumentis; et quasi hoc exponens adiecit, Et herbam servitude hominum: ne non intelligeres quod dictum est, Producens fenum iumentis, repetitione exposuit quod praemisit. Quod enim dixit supra fenum, post herbam nominavit; quod autem dixerat iumentis, hoc servitude hominum dixit. Etgo servituti, et non libertati. Ubi ergo est, Vos in libertatem vocati estis?
